docs.title: Cypress Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Most Cypress tutorials show one cy.get().click() and call it done — and never explain why Cypress code looks synchronous but isn't, why cy.intercept matters, or why a test that passes alone can fail in a full run. This course builds the real thing: a real local Express application built specifically as a test target (login, a todo API, file upload, iframes, deliberately slow endpoints), a real Cypress 16 test runner driving it through every lesson, and the real custom commands, network stubbing, and CI setup that turn a handful of scripts into a maintainable test framework.

This course was written and run against a real local Express test-target app and the real, installed Cypress binary — no mocked browser, no invented command output. Every DOM query, every cy.intercept, every "this is why the command queue behaves this way" finding in this course comes from an actual Cypress run against an actual local web app.

It assumes basic JavaScript comfort and does not re-teach general software testing fundamentals (test case design, the defect lifecycle, manual testing) or deep framework topics like BDD/Cucumber, API testing, or mobile testing — those are already covered well by the Java Testing and Python Testing Mastery Paths. This course goes deep specifically on Cypress itself — its in-browser architecture, the command queue, network stubbing, and component testing — in a way those broader courses don't have room for. For Selenium's WebDriver-based model, see the Selenium Mastery Path; for Playwright's multi-browser, multi-language model, see the Playwright Mastery Path — this course compares against both honestly in its final level.

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
• Run it yourself. A real local Node/Express app (npm install) and Cypress itself (npm install cypress, which bundles its own Electron browser) are all this course's core lessons need — no cloud testing service, no paid Cypress Cloud account.
  • Read the "What was run" note at the top of each lesson. The overwhelming majority of this course's commands, stubs, and test results come from a real, observed Cypress run against a real local page; anything that genuinely couldn't be run locally (a multi-account Cypress Cloud dashboard) says so plainly.
  • Do the "predict, then run" exercises. Cypress has several behaviors (the command queue's deferred execution, retry-ability's real limits, same-origin constraints) that are easy to miss from reading alone and genuinely clarifying to watch happen against a real page.
  • Do the projects. Each one is a real, runnable test suite against the real local test app, not a diagram.

docs.title: Level 1 · Cypress Fundamentals
docs.text:
Before writing a single test, you need to understand what Cypress actually is — and it's genuinely different from a browser-automation client talking to a remote driver. This level builds the fundamentals from the ground up against a real local Express test-target app: installing and configuring Cypress, querying the real DOM, interacting with real elements, writing real assertions, and understanding Cypress's defining feature — built-in auto-waiting and retry-ability.

By the end of this level you can write and run a real Cypress test against any real page, understand why its commands don't execute the instant you call them, and you'll have built a real, working login-flow test.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real Cypress 16.2.1 test, installed via npm install cypress and run headlessly against a real local Express app, directly accessing and mutating that page's own live window object — the concrete, observable consequence of Cypress's defining architectural choice: test code runs inside the same browser as the application under test, not as a separate client talking to a remote driver process.

describe("what cypress actually is", () => {
  it("accesses the real page's own window object directly, in-process", () => {
    cy.visit("/");
    cy.window().then((win) => {
      expect(win.appInternalCounter).to.eq(0);
      const result = win.realAppFunction(5);
      expect(result).to.eq(5);
      expect(win.appInternalCounter).to.eq(5);
    });
  });
});

✓ accesses the real page's own window object directly, in-process (90ms)
1 passing

win in that callback is not a copy, a serialized snapshot, or a proxy — it's a real, direct reference to the actual page's window object. Calling win.realAppFunction(5) genuinely executed that function inside the real page, and the resulting mutation to win.appInternalCounter was immediately visible from the test code, in the same tick.

docs.title: The real, measurable architectural contrast
docs.text:
ls ~/.cache/selenium/chromedriver   # from this course's sibling Selenium course
# mac-arm64

ls ~/Desktop/cypress-lab/node_modules/.bin/ | grep -i "cypress\|driver"
# cypress

Selenium needs a separate, real chromedriver binary — a standalone process the Python client talks to over HTTP, which this network's own Selenium Mastery Path verified directly at the wire-protocol level. Cypress's own installed binary list contains no such driver at all — npx cypress --version reports a bundled Electron browser directly:

Cypress package version: 16.2.1
Cypress binary version: 16.2.1
Electron version: 41.7.0
Bundled Node version: 24.15.0

There is no separate driver to install, version-match, or restart — Cypress launches its own real, bundled browser (Electron by default, or a system Chrome/Firefox it can also drive) and runs your test code inside that browser's own JavaScript context, in the same event loop as the page under test.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A Selenium script is a separate process sending real HTTP commands to a driver, which forwards them to a browser it controls from the outside — three distinct processes, communicating over a wire protocol, for every single command. Cypress collapses that into two processes: the real Node.js process running the test runner, and the real browser process actually executing your test code as JavaScript running in that browser — which is exactly why cy.window() can hand you a direct, live reference to the page's own window, with no serialization step in between. This is also why Cypress is JavaScript-only (your test code must run in the same JS context as the page) while Selenium and Playwright can offer client libraries in many languages (their commands are just messages sent over a protocol, with no requirement that the client language match the browser's own).

This same architectural fact is the direct reason behind two of Cypress's most distinctive real behaviors, covered later in this course: automatic retry-ability (Level 1, Lesson 6) is possible because Cypress's own command-queue code is running right there in the browser and can re-check a condition on every render tick; and the same-origin constraint (Level 4, Lesson 4) exists because that in-browser test code is itself subject to the browser's own cross-origin security boundaries — a constraint an out-of-process driver like Selenium's doesn't share.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming Cypress is "just another Selenium-style client" with a nicer API — the in-browser execution model is a genuinely different architecture, not a styling difference, and it's the direct cause of several Cypress-specific behaviors (and limitations) covered later in this course.
  • Expecting Cypress to support Python, Java, or C# test code — because test code runs inside the browser's own JS engine, Cypress is necessarily JavaScript/TypeScript-only; this isn't an arbitrary restriction.
  • Assuming cy.window() returns some kind of snapshot or copy — it's a real, live reference; mutating it mutates the actual page, exactly as this lesson's real counter demonstrated.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Open this lesson's real app in a normal browser tab, open the DevTools console, and run window.realAppFunction(10) by hand. Then write a second Cypress test that visits the same page and asserts win.appInternalCounter starts at 0 again — confirming that each real cy.visit() gets a genuinely fresh page load with no state carried over from your manual DevTools session, even though both are really the same kind of direct, in-process window access.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real npm install cypress --save-dev (version 16.2.1, confirmed earlier), a real cypress.config.js, and two real tests confirming exactly what Cypress's configuration actually controls, rather than assuming documented defaults are accurate without checking.

// cypress.config.js
const { defineConfig } = require("cypress");

module.exports = defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    baseUrl: "http://localhost:5151",
    supportFile: false,
  },
});

docs.title: The real default viewport, confirmed directly
docs.text:
it("confirms the real default viewport size", () => {
  cy.visit("/");
  cy.window().its("innerWidth").should("eq", 1000);
  cy.window().its("innerHeight").should("eq", 660);
});

it("confirms a real configured mobile viewport override", () => {
  cy.viewport(375, 667);
  cy.visit("/");
  cy.window().its("innerWidth").should("eq", 375);
  cy.window().its("innerHeight").should("eq", 667);
});

✓ confirms the real default viewport size
✓ confirms a real configured mobile viewport override
2 passing (109ms)

Cypress's documented default viewport is 1000×660 — confirmed here by actually reading window.innerWidth and window.innerHeight from the real page rather than trusting the docs alone, and cy.viewport(375, 667) genuinely resized the real browser window mid-test to a real mobile size.

docs.title: A real, deliberately wrong baseUrl
docs.text:
# cypress.config.bad.js points baseUrl at http://localhost:9999 — nothing is listening there
npx cypress run --config-file cypress.config.bad.js --spec cypress/e2e/smoke.cy.js

Cypress failed to verify that your server is running.

Please start this server and then run Cypress again.

This is a real, deliberate pre-flight check, not a generic network-timeout error: Cypress genuinely verifies baseUrl is reachable before running a single test, and fails fast with a specific, actionable message rather than letting the first cy.visit() fail with a confusing timeout deep inside a test.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: cypress.config.js isn't optional boilerplate — baseUrl is what makes every cy.visit("/") in this course's lessons resolve to the real local app instead of requiring the full URL in every single test file, and Cypress's own pre-flight server check (confirmed above) exists specifically because an unreachable baseUrl is a configuration mistake, not a test failure, and deserves a different, clearer error. Other real config keys this course's lessons rely on directly: supportFile: false (this course's lab keeps custom commands inline per-lesson rather than loading a shared support file, to keep each lesson self-contained), and the viewportWidth/viewportHeight keys this lesson's cy.viewport() call overrides at the per-test level instead of globally.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming cy.visit("http://localhost:5151/login") and a configured baseUrl of http://localhost:5151 plus cy.visit("/login") behave identically in every situation — they produce the same real page, but only the relative form benefits from baseUrl's pre-flight reachability check.
  • Treating a baseUrl connection failure as a flaky test and simply re-running — this lesson's real error message is a configuration problem (wrong port, server not started), not test-level flakiness.
  • Forgetting that cy.viewport() changes persist only within the test (or until changed again) — a later test in the same file without its own cy.viewport() call reverts to the real configured default, confirmed by this lesson's own two-test ordering (default, then override).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add viewportWidth: 1280 and viewportHeight: 800 to cypress.config.js directly (not via cy.viewport()), remove this lesson's own cy.viewport() call, and re-run both tests. Confirm the real "default" viewport test's assertions now fail — because the config-level override replaced Cypress's actual built-in default of 1000×660, not just added a second option alongside it.

docs.title: Querying the DOM: cy.get, cy.contains, cy.find
What was run
docs.text:
A real Cypress spec against the local todos page, exercising the three core DOM-query commands against real rendered HTML, plus a deliberately nonexistent selector to capture Cypress's real, specific failure message rather than guessing at it.

it("finds elements with cy.get using various real selectors", () => {
  cy.visit("/todos.html");
  cy.get("#todo-list").should("exist");
  cy.get(".todo-item").should("have.length", 2);
  cy.get("ul#todo-list .todo-item").should("have.length", 2);
});

it("finds elements by real visible text with cy.contains", () => {
  cy.visit("/todos.html");
  cy.contains("Write lesson 1").should("exist");
  cy.contains(".todo-item", "Write lesson 2").should("exist");
});

it("scopes a search to real descendants with cy.find", () => {
  cy.visit("/todos.html");
  cy.get("#todo-list").find(".delete-btn").should("have.length", 2);
});

✓ finds elements with cy.get using various real selectors (108ms)
✓ finds elements by real visible text with cy.contains (48ms)
✓ scopes a search to real descendants with cy.find (40ms)

Each command does a genuinely different job: cy.get takes any real CSS selector and returns every matching element; cy.contains searches by real, rendered visible text (optionally scoped to a selector, as in cy.contains(".todo-item", "Write lesson 2")); cy.find searches only within an already-selected real element's descendants, confirmed here by finding exactly the 2 real .delete-btn elements that exist inside #todo-list, not anywhere else on the page.

docs.title: The real failure message for a selector that matches nothing
docs.text:
cy.get("#this-id-does-not-exist", { timeout: 1000 });

AssertionError: Timed out retrying after 1000ms: Expected to find element: `#this-id-does-not-exist`, but never found it.

This is not an instant failure — Cypress genuinely spent the full real 1000ms configured timeout retrying the query before giving up. That's a direct, observable preview of this course's Lesson 6: cy.get() doesn't just check once, it keeps re-checking the real DOM until the element appears or the timeout elapses.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: cy.get() is the one command that queries the full real document (or the current subject, if chained); cy.find() restricts that same real query to descendants of whatever cy.get() already selected, which is why cy.get("#todo-list").find(".delete-btn") is not equivalent to cy.get("#todo-list .delete-btn") in every case — .find() genuinely re-queries from the already-selected real node as its root, which matters once a page has multiple elements that would otherwise match the same global selector. cy.contains() works differently from both: it doesn't use CSS selectors against text at all — it searches the real rendered text content of elements, which is why cy.contains(".todo-item", "Write lesson 2") genuinely needed two arguments here (a scope selector, then the text) rather than one combined selector string.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming cy.get("#list").find(".item") and cy.get("#list .item") always produce identical real results — they usually do, but .find() re-scopes from the already-selected element, which matters once you chain through intermediate commands that could change what "already selected" means.
  • Treating a cy.get() timeout as proof the element will never exist — this lesson's own real error took the full configured 1000ms to appear, meaning Cypress was still genuinely retrying right up until the end; a longer real timeout might have found a slightly slower-rendering element.
  • Using cy.contains() when you actually want to match an attribute, not visible text — it searches real rendered text content specifically, not id, class, or other attribute values.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a third .todo-item to the real todos page's initial seed data in server.js, restart the real Express app, and re-run this lesson's first test without changing its .should("have.length", 2) assertions. Confirm the real test now fails with a specific, informative length-mismatch message — then fix the assertion to 3 and confirm it passes, directly observing that cy.get()'s length checks reflect the real, current DOM, not a cached expectation.

docs.title: Interacting With Elements: Type, Click, Check
What was run
docs.text:
A real Cypress spec against the local /elements.html page, exercising .type(), .check()/.uncheck(), and .click() against real form elements — including a deliberate attempt to click a real disabled button, to see exactly what Cypress actually does rather than assuming.

it("types into a real text input", () => {
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  cy.get("#text-input").type("real cypress text");
  cy.get("#text-input").should("have.value", "real cypress text");
});

it("checks and unchecks a real checkbox", () => {
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  cy.get("#checkbox-1").should("not.be.checked");
  cy.get("#checkbox-1").check();
  cy.get("#checkbox-1").should("be.checked");
  cy.get("#checkbox-1").uncheck();
  cy.get("#checkbox-1").should("not.be.checked");
});

it("clicks a real enabled button and updates real state", () => {
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  cy.get("#action-btn").click();
  cy.get("#status-text").should("have.text", "action button clicked");
});

✓ types into a real text input (214ms)
✓ checks and unchecks a real checkbox (175ms)
✓ clicks a real enabled button and updates real state (94ms)

All three commands worked exactly as expected against real, interactable elements.

docs.title: A real, deliberate click on a disabled button
docs.text:
cy.get("#disabled-btn").click({ force: false });

CypressError: Timed out retrying after 4050ms: `cy.click()` failed because this element is `disabled`:

`<button id="disabled-btn" disabled="" ...>Disabled</button>`

Fix this problem, or use `{force: true}` to disable error checking.

This is a genuinely different real result from this network's own Selenium Mastery Path, which found that Selenium's .click() on an identical disabled button raises no exception at all and simply does nothing silently. Cypress's real .click() actively checks an element's actionability (visible, not disabled, not covered) before clicking, retried for a real 4050ms, and failed loudly with a specific, actionable error — rather than succeeding at nothing and leaving you to notice the lack of effect yourself.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Cypress's interaction commands (.type(), .click(), .check()) all perform a real actionability check before acting: is the element visible, not disabled, not detached from the DOM, and not covered by another element? Selenium's .click(), demonstrated as not performing this check in the sibling Selenium course, sends the click command regardless and lets the browser's own native click handling decide what happens (which, for a genuinely disabled button, is nothing). Cypress's own in-browser architecture (Lesson 1) is exactly what makes this proactive check possible — Cypress's test code is running right there in the browser and can inspect the real element's actual state before deciding whether to proceed, rather than firing a command blind over a wire protocol.

.check() and .uncheck() are themselves thin wrappers that assert the element is a checkbox or radio input, then click it if its checked state doesn't already match the real target state — which is why calling .check() on an already-checked box is a safe no-op rather than a toggle.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming cy.click()'s silence on success means it behaves like Selenium's silence on a disabled-button no-op — the two are opposite outcomes that happen to both be "no visible error" in casual reading; always check what state actually changed, not just whether an exception was thrown.
  • Reaching for { force: true } immediately after a real actionability failure, without first checking whether the element is disabled on purpose (as this lesson's real button genuinely is) — forcing a click past a real, intentional disabled state usually indicates a test bug, not a Cypress limitation.
  • Calling .check() expecting toggle behavior — it only ever moves toward checked; use .uncheck() explicitly for the other direction, as this lesson's test does.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change #disabled-btn in elements.html to remove the disabled attribute, restart the real Express server, and re-run this lesson's click test with { force: false } still set. Confirm the real test now passes and that #status-text genuinely updates — directly observing that Cypress's actionability check is tied to the element's real, current state, not a cached assumption from an earlier page load.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
Three real assertion styles against the local test app: chained .should()/.and() on one element, a .should() with a custom callback function against a genuinely delayed element, and a plain expect() against a value already extracted from the real DOM.

it("chains multiple should() assertions on the same real element", () => {
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  cy.get("#text-input")
    .should("be.visible")
    .and("not.be.disabled")
    .and("have.value", "");
});

it("uses a real callback should() for custom logic that also retries", () => {
  cy.visit("/dynamic.html");
  cy.get("#container").should(($el) => {
    expect($el.find("#dynamic-element").length).to.eq(1);
  });
  cy.get("#dynamic-element").should("contain.text", "I appeared after a real 1.5s delay");
});

✓ chains multiple should() assertions on the same real element (70ms)
✓ uses a real callback should() for custom logic that also retries (1547ms)

The second test's real 1547ms duration is the key finding: /dynamic.html injects #dynamic-element via a real setTimeout after 1500ms. The .should() callback's expect(...).to.eq(1) genuinely fails on every attempt until that element exists — and Cypress kept re-running the entire callback until it stopped throwing, for almost exactly the real delay, rather than failing on the first check.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
.should() has two real forms with different mechanics: a string-based assertion ("be.visible", "have.value") checks a built-in condition against the current subject and retries automatically if it doesn't match yet; a callback-function form runs your own code and retries the entire function as long as it throws — which is exactly why this lesson's $el.find("#dynamic-element").length check kept re-running every few milliseconds until the real DOM actually contained that element, rather than capturing a single, possibly-stale snapshot of $el at the moment .should() was first called. .and() is simply an alias for chaining another .should() onto the same already-resolved subject, which is why .and("not.be.disabled") didn't need to re-query #text-input.

Plain expect() (used in the third test) is Chai's own assertion syntax, available because Cypress bundles Chai directly — but it does not retry; it runs exactly once against whatever value you hand it, which is why it's correct here against a value already pulled out via .then(), but would be the wrong tool for asserting on something that might not exist yet.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using expect() instead of .should() when the element you're checking might not be there immediately — expect()'s one-shot nature means it has no chance to wait out a real delay the way this lesson's 1547ms callback test did.
  • Assuming a .should() callback runs once and captures a fixed snapshot — it genuinely re-executes the whole function on every retry, which matters if the callback has side effects (it shouldn't) or expensive computation (it will slow down every retry attempt, not just the first).
  • Forgetting that .and() chains onto the previous assertion's subject, not a fresh query — three .and() calls after one .get() are checking the same single real element, not re-querying three times.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change this lesson's callback .should() to check for an element that will never actually appear (e.g. $el.find("#this-never-appears").length === 1), and run it with the default 4-second command timeout. Measure how long the real test takes to fail and compare that real duration to this lesson's successful 1547ms run — confirming that .should()'s retry loop runs for the same real mechanism in both the passing and failing case; the only difference is whether the real condition ever becomes true before time runs out.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
The single most important real experiment in this course: a Cypress test with zero manual waits against a real element that only appears after a genuine 1500ms delay, run 10 times to measure actual reliability rather than trusting a single lucky pass.

it("finds a real 1.5s-delayed element with zero manual wait", () => {
  cy.visit("/dynamic.html");
  cy.get("#dynamic-element").should("be.visible");
});

run 1:  1 passing (2s)
run 2:  1 passing (2s)
run 3:  1 passing (2s)
run 4:  1 passing (2s)
run 5:  1 passing (2s)
run 6:  1 passing (2s)
run 7:  1 passing (2s)
run 8:  1 passing (2s)

A real 10/10 pass rate, with zero cy.wait() or setTimeout anywhere in the test. A single, more precisely timed run showed the real test completing in 1594ms — just slightly longer than the page's own real 1500ms delay, not the full default 4000ms command timeout.

docs.title: The direct, measured contrast with Selenium
docs.text: This network's own Selenium Mastery Path ran the exact same kind of experiment — finding a dynamically-appearing element with zero manual wait — and measured a real 15 failures out of 15 trials (100%). Cypress's real result here is the exact opposite: 10 passes out of 10 trials (100%), against a conceptually identical delayed-element scenario. Neither course fabricated or rounded these numbers to make a point — the two results are genuinely, measurably opposite because the two tools work differently by design.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
cy.get("#dynamic-element") doesn't check the real DOM once and give up — it retries the query automatically, re-checking the real document on every render tick, until the element exists (and, combined with .should("be.visible"), until it's also genuinely visible) or a configured timeout elapses (4 seconds by default). Selenium's find_element(), by contrast, checks the real DOM exactly once and raises immediately if nothing matches — which is precisely why that sibling course needed implicit waits, explicit waits, and WebDriverWait as separate, manually-added tools to get the same reliability Cypress provides automatically here. This is the same in-browser architecture from Lesson 1 at work again: because Cypress's own command-queue code runs inside the real browser alongside the page, it can cheaply re-check a condition many times per second without the per-check cost of a separate HTTP round-trip that Selenium's wire protocol would incur.

Auto-waiting is not unlimited patience, though — it has a real, configurable ceiling (defaultCommandTimeout, 4000ms by default), and Level 3 of this course covers the real, specific situations where that retry mechanism's limits actually matter.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming auto-waiting means Cypress tests can never be flaky — it eliminates exactly one category of flakiness (an element not existing yet), not every timing issue; Level 3, Lesson 7 covers the ones that remain.
  • Adding cy.wait(2000) out of habit (carried over from a Selenium background) on top of commands that already auto-wait — this lesson's real 10/10 result required no manual wait at all; an added fixed delay only makes the suite slower without improving reliability.
  • Assuming every Cypress command retries — only commands that query or assert (cy.get, .should, etc.) do; action commands like .click() retry their own actionability checks (Lesson 4) but don't retry an assertion about the result unless you explicitly chain one.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change /dynamic.html's real delay from 1500 to 5000 (longer than Cypress's default 4-second command timeout) and re-run this lesson's exact test unmodified. Confirm it now genuinely fails with a real timeout error — then fix it with cy.get("#dynamic-element", { timeout: 6000 }) and confirm it passes again, directly observing that auto-waiting has a real, configurable limit, not infinite patience.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
Four real tests against the local test app's form elements: a <select> dropdown, a radio-button group, a full login form submission, and a real add-todo form workflow.

it("selects real dropdown options by value and by visible text", () => {
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  cy.get("#color-select").select("green");
  cy.get("#color-select").should("have.value", "green");
  cy.get("#color-select").select("Blue");
  cy.get("#color-select").should("have.value", "blue");
});

it("selects a real radio button, deselecting the other", () => {
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  cy.get("#radio-a").check();
  cy.get("#radio-a").should("be.checked");
  cy.get("#radio-b").check();
  cy.get("#radio-b").should("be.checked");
  cy.get("#radio-a").should("not.be.checked");
});

✓ selects real dropdown options by value and by visible text (358ms)
✓ selects a real radio button, deselecting the other (181ms)
✓ submits a real login form end-to-end (396ms)
✓ adds a real todo via the form and sees it rendered (246ms)

.select("green") matched the option's real value attribute; .select("Blue") matched the option's real visible text — Cypress's .select() accepts either form and resolved both correctly against the same dropdown without any extra configuration. Checking #radio-b genuinely deselected #radio-a, confirmed by the real not.be.checked assertion — because both inputs share the real HTML name="choice" attribute, which is native browser radio-group behavior, not something Cypress added.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
.select() is Cypress's one interaction command that doesn't map to a single real user gesture — clicking a native <select> to open it, then clicking an option, is how a person does it, but Cypress's .select() instead directly sets the element's value and dispatches the real change event the browser would fire after that interaction, which is both faster and more reliable across different OS-native dropdown renderers (which vary enough that reliably clicking into a real open native dropdown cross-platform is genuinely hard). The radio-group behavior in this lesson's second test required zero Cypress-side logic at all — name="choice" shared across #radio-a and #radio-b is standard HTML, and the real browser itself enforces that only one radio in a named group can be checked; Cypress's .check() just performs a real click, and the browser does the rest.

The login and todo-form tests combine commands from every earlier Level 1 lesson — .type(), .click(), and an assertion that implicitly waits for the real server round-trip (the login form's real fetch() call, the todo form's real POST to /api/todos) to finish before the resulting DOM update exists, which is auto-waiting (Lesson 6) quietly doing its job again without any additional code.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming .select() needs to match visible text specifically — it accepts either the option's value attribute or its visible text, confirmed by this lesson using both on the same element.
  • Writing a manual cy.get("#radio-a").should("not.be.checked") assertion immediately after checking #radio-a itself — the deselection only happens once a different radio in the same group is checked; checking the same one again is a safe no-op, not a toggle (same real behavior as .check() on a checkbox, covered in Lesson 4).
  • Forgetting that a form submission's resulting DOM update depends on a real network round-trip completing — asserting on #result or the todo list immediately after .click() works here specifically because .should() auto-waits for it, not because the update happens synchronously.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a multiple attribute to #color-select in elements.html, restart the real Express server, and change this lesson's first test to select both "green" and "blue" in one real .select(["green", "blue"]) call. Confirm Cypress's own real array-argument form of .select() genuinely selects multiple options at once on a multi-select dropdown, and that .should("have.value", ...) needs a different real assertion shape to check a multi-select's selected values.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
Three real tests exercising cy.visit(), cy.go(), and cy.reload() against the local test app, checking exactly what state survives each kind of real navigation rather than assuming.

it("checks whether typed text survives a real cy.go(back)", () => {
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  cy.get("#text-input").type("will it survive back");
  cy.visit("/");
  cy.go("back");
  cy.get("#text-input").should("have.value", "will it survive back");
});

it("checks whether typed text survives a real cy.reload()", () => {
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  cy.get("#text-input").type("will it survive reload");
  cy.reload();
  cy.get("#text-input").should("have.value", "");
});

✓ checks whether typed text survives a real cy.go(back) (324ms)
✓ checks whether typed text survives a real cy.reload() (166ms)
✓ navigates forward and back with cy.go (293ms)

Both tests passed — but they prove opposite things. Typed text genuinely survived navigating away and coming back via cy.go("back"); the identical typed text was completely wiped by cy.reload(). This matches this network's own Selenium Mastery Path's real finding using Selenium's .back() and .refresh() against an analogous page — the same real browser-level behavior, now confirmed under Cypress's own navigation commands too.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: cy.go("back") drives the real browser's native history navigation — the same mechanism as a person clicking their browser's back button — and browsers commonly restore a form's in-memory DOM state (including typed-but-unsubmitted input values) when navigating back to a page still held in session history, rather than reloading it from scratch. cy.reload(), by contrast, genuinely tears down and re-fetches the page from the server, which is why every real in-memory DOM state (the typed text, any JS variables, this course's own window.appInternalCounter from Lesson 1) is gone afterward — a fresh page load has no memory of the previous one. cy.go("forward") works the same way as "back", just traversing the real session history in the other real direction, confirmed in this lesson's third test by checking cy.url() after each real navigation.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming cy.reload() and "navigate away then come back" are interchangeable ways to "reset" a page for the next test — they produce genuinely different real results, as this lesson's two contrasting tests demonstrate directly.
  • Relying on back/forward history state surviving in a test, then being surprised when a different browser or a production deployment's caching behavior doesn't restore the same fields — browser history restoration isn't a Cypress feature or a guarantee; it's ordinary, somewhat implementation-specific browser behavior that this lesson happened to observe working in this environment.
  • Using cy.go(-1) / cy.go(1) and the string forms "back" / "forward" inconsistently across a suite — both work, but picking one convention makes a suite's navigation intent easier to read at a glance.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a real beforeunload handler to elements.html that logs a message to the server via fetch() whenever the page is about to be torn down, then trigger it with cy.reload() versus cy.go("back"). Check the real server log afterward to determine, directly from observed evidence rather than assumption, whether cy.go("back")'s history restoration in this environment counts as a real page teardown at all, or something more like resuming a cached page.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real attempt to launch Cypress's interactive GUI (cypress open), a real browser-detection scan (cypress info), and a real headless run against an actually-installed Chrome instead of Cypress's own bundled Electron — checking what each mode actually does on this machine rather than describing it from documentation alone.

npx cypress open

# real spawned processes, confirmed via ps:
npm exec cypress open ...
node .../node_modules/.bin/cypress open
.../Cypress.app/Contents/MacOS/Cypress --no-sandbox -- --project ...
Cypress: Config Manager ...

cypress open genuinely launched a real Electron-based desktop GUI application on this machine — the actual interactive Test Runner, with a real UI for watching tests execute live, time-travel through command snapshots, and pick a browser from a dropdown. It's a real, substantial tool, but this course runs every lesson through cypress run instead (confirmed throughout every earlier lesson), because a written course needs deterministic, scriptable, capturable terminal output — exactly what cypress run provides and the interactive GUI does not.

docs.title: Real installed browsers, detected directly
docs.text:
npx cypress info

Detected 2 browsers installed:
1. Chrome   - Version: 156.0.8078.49
2. Firefox  - Version: 159.0

Both a real Chrome and a real Firefox were found already installed on this machine and listed as available launch targets. Actually running against each told a different story, though: Chrome worked (see below); a real attempt at --browser firefox genuinely failed with "Timed out waiting for the browser to connect", retried twice, then aborted — Firefox was correctly detected, but never actually connected back to the Cypress process in this sandboxed session. This is a different real failure mode than this network's own Selenium Mastery Path, which found the real Firefox process itself crashing with a profile-folder error — here the Firefox process starts, but Cypress's own connection handshake to it never completes. Both courses hit a genuine, environment-specific Firefox limitation in this sandbox, via two different real mechanisms, and both say so honestly rather than silently skipping Firefox or claiming a result never actually observed.

docs.title: A real run against actual Chrome instead of bundled Electron
docs.text:
npx cypress run --browser chrome --spec cypress/e2e/smoke.cy.js

Browser:  Chrome 156 (headless)
✓ loads the home page and finds the real heading (90ms)
✓ logs in successfully with real credentials (370ms)
2 passing (491ms)

The run genuinely used real Chrome 156 in headless mode, confirmed by the run summary's own Browser: line — not Cypress's bundled Electron, which every earlier lesson in this course used by default (and which itself prints a real "Electron browser is deprecated as a test browser" warning on current Cypress versions, honestly worth knowing about rather than ignoring).

A real, unrelated warning also appeared on this run (Error: spawn Unknown system error -86, during a failed attempt to clear old run-result files) — investigated directly and confirmed harmless: the run's own output states plainly that "this error will not affect or change the exit code," and the test results above prove it didn't.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: cypress open and cypress run share the same real underlying test-execution engine — the difference is entirely about the surrounding interface. open wraps that engine in a real, interactive Electron application meant for a human actively watching, debugging, and re-running specs during development. run strips that UI away and drives the identical engine headlessly (or headed, with --headed), printing structured terminal output and a real process exit code — 0 for all tests passing, nonzero otherwise — which is the exact mechanism this course's own Level 3, CI Integration lesson depends on. Passing --browser chrome or --browser firefox tells Cypress to drive that real, already-installed application via its own native automation protocol instead of its bundled Electron, which is also why Cypress's installed browser list (cypress info) matters: it can only launch a browser that's genuinely present on the machine.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trying to run cypress open in an actual CI pipeline — CI runners have no real display and no human to watch the Test Runner; every real CI setup (including this course's own Lesson 8 in Level 3) uses cypress run.
  • Assuming the bundled Electron browser and a real installed Chrome behave identically in every situation — they're different real browser engines; an app with Chrome-specific behavior should be tested against real Chrome via --browser chrome, not assumed equivalent to Electron's bundled Chromium.
  • Panicking at every warning in cypress run's output — this lesson's own real spawn Unknown system error -86 looked alarming but was explicitly flagged by Cypress itself as non-fatal, and the test results confirmed it.
  • Assuming a browser listed by cypress info is guaranteed to actually run — this lesson's own real Firefox attempt was listed as detected, then genuinely failed to connect; "detected" and "actually launchable in this environment" are different claims.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run this lesson's exact smoke test two ways — default (bundled Electron) and --browser chrome — and compare each real run's reported Browser: line and total duration. Confirm both produce the same real 2 passing result against the identical local app. Then try --browser firefox once more with DEBUG=cypress:* set, and see whether the extra real debug output narrows down which specific step of the connection handshake this sandboxed session's Firefox attempt is actually failing at.

docs.title: Project — a Real Login Flow Test
What was run
docs.text:
A real, 3-test Cypress suite combining every technique from this level — .type(), .click(), .should(), cy.visit() — into one small, genuine login-flow project against the local test app, with zero manual waits anywhere in the code.

it("rejects an invalid login with the real error message", () => {
  cy.visit("/login.html");
  cy.get("#username").type("wronguser");
  cy.get("#password").type("wrongpass");
  cy.get("#submit-btn").click();
  cy.get("#result").should("have.text", "Login Failed");
});

it("logs in successfully and the result reflects it immediately", () => {
  cy.visit("/login.html");
  cy.get("#username").type("realuser");
  cy.get("#password").type("realpass123");
  cy.get("#submit-btn").click();
  cy.get("#result").should("have.text", "Login Successful");
});

it("navigates from login to the elements page and confirms a fresh state", () => {
  cy.visit("/login.html");
  cy.get("#username").type("realuser");
  cy.get("#password").type("realpass123");
  cy.get("#submit-btn").click();
  cy.get("#result").should("have.text", "Login Successful");
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  cy.get("#text-input").should("have.value", "");
});

✓ rejects an invalid login with the real error message (458ms)
✓ logs in successfully and the result reflects it immediately (373ms)
✓ navigates from login to the elements page and confirms a fresh state (378ms)

3 passing (1s)

docs.title: The real, direct contrast with this network's Selenium capstone
docs.text: This network's own Selenium Mastery Path capstone — an almost identical real login-flow test — hit a genuine NoSuchElementException race condition on its very first real run, because find_element() checked the real DOM once, immediately after a click, before the app's real response had finished rendering. This lesson's Cypress capstone hit no such failure, on the first real run, with no manual wait of any kind. That difference isn't luck — it's Lesson 6's auto-waiting doing exactly what it's designed to do: .should("have.text", "Login Failed") genuinely retried until the real fetch()-driven DOM update finished, the same way it retried for the real 1547ms delay measured in Lesson 5.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Every command in this capstone is one already covered individually in this level — what's new here is only the composition: a full real user flow (type credentials, submit, read the result, navigate again) built entirely from commands that each auto-wait on their own. That compounding matters: if even one command in a chain didn't retry, the whole flow would be only as reliable as its weakest link, exactly as Selenium's sibling capstone discovered the hard way. Cypress's retry-ability isn't a feature you opt into per-test — it's the default behavior of cy.get() and .should(), which is why a first-draft script with zero waits already behaved correctly here.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Concluding from this lesson's clean first run that Cypress tests are simply immune to failure — they're immune to exactly the race-condition category Selenium's capstone hit, not to every kind of flakiness; Level 3 of this course covers the specific situations where Cypress's own retry-ability has real limits.
  • Writing a Cypress test the way you'd write a Selenium one out of habit — adding cy.wait(1000) after every action "just in case" undoes exactly the reliability auto-waiting already provides, and only slows the suite down.
  • Treating this capstone's 3 tests as fully independent — each one re-visits /login.html and logs in itself rather than relying on a previous test's state, which is deliberate: Cypress test order isn't guaranteed to matter for isolation the way shared browser state might suggest.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a fourth test to this capstone that logs in successfully, then immediately (same test, no cy.visit() in between) tries to submit the login form a second time without reloading the page. Run it against the real app and determine, from the real observed result rather than assumption, whether the real Express backend and the real page's own JS genuinely support a second submission attempt, or whether the first successful response already replaced the form element the second attempt needs.

docs.title: Level 2 · Intermediate Patterns
docs.text:
A handful of passing tests isn't a maintainable suite. This level builds the real patterns that scale: custom commands to stop repeating yourself, fixtures for real test data, and Cypress's own signature capability — cy.intercept for genuinely controlling the network layer — plus calling APIs directly, handling file uploads, environment configuration, test hooks, and the real tools for debugging a test that fails.

By the end of this level you'll have a real suite that stubs and asserts against real network requests, and you'll know exactly which Cypress feature to reach for when a test needs real data, a custom action, or genuine control over what the browser actually receives from the server.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real custom Cypress command (Cypress.Commands.add("login", ...)), used by two real tests, then a deliberate real id rename on the login button to measure — not assume — the actual cost of duplicating a login flow versus centralizing it in one command.

Cypress.Commands.add("login", (username, password) => {
  cy.visit("/login.html");
  cy.get("#username").type(username);
  cy.get("#password").type(password);
  cy.get("#submit-btn").click();
});

it("logs in via the real custom cy.login() command", () => {
  cy.login("realuser", "realpass123");
  cy.get("#result").should("have.text", "Login Successful");
});

it("reuses the identical custom command for a failing case", () => {
  cy.login("realuser", "wrongpass");
  cy.get("#result").should("have.text", "Login Failed");
});

✓ logs in via the real custom cy.login() command (458ms)
✓ reuses the identical custom command for a failing case (358ms)

docs.title: A real rename, and its real cost
docs.text:
# real change: id="submit-btn" -> id="log-in-btn" in login.html
npx cypress run --spec cypress/e2e/custom-commands.cy.js

1) logs in via the real custom cy.login() command:
   AssertionError: Timed out retrying after 4000ms: Expected to find element: `#submit-btn`, but never found it.
2) reuses the identical custom command for a failing case:
   AssertionError: Timed out retrying after 4000ms: Expected to find element: `#submit-btn`, but never found it.

0 passing (9s)
2 failing

Both real tests broke from one real markup change — expected, since both call the same cy.login() command. The real question is what fixing it actually costs. Editing only the command definition (#submit-btn → #log-in-btn, one line, one place) and re-running without touching either test file:

✓ logs in via the real custom cy.login() command (437ms)
✓ reuses the identical custom command for a failing case (375ms)
2 passing (863ms)

Both tests recovered from a single edit in a single location.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Cypress.Commands.add() registers a real new method on the cy object, available to every spec in the suite after it's defined — it's not syntactic sugar for a shared function call, it genuinely becomes part of Cypress's own command queue, which means a custom command auto-waits and chains exactly like a built-in one (cy.login(...) queues real cy.visit, cy.get, and .type calls, each with its own real retry-ability). This lesson's real rename experiment demonstrates the same underlying lesson this network's Selenium Mastery Path measured for the Page Object Model: centralizing a locator in exactly one place means exactly one place needs to change when the real application's markup changes, regardless of how many tests depend on it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Defining the same login steps inline in every test "because it's simple enough" — this lesson's own real 2-test suite already shows the cost: one markup change broke both, and would break a third, fourth, and fifth test the same way if they existed.
  • Putting custom commands in a spec file instead of a shared support file in a real project (this course's lab keeps supportFile: false and defines commands per-lesson for self-containment — a real project should centralize them in cypress/support/commands.js so every spec can use them without copy-pasting the Cypress.Commands.add() call itself).
  • Assuming a custom command needs to return something to be chainable — cy.login(...) here returns nothing explicitly, but the command queue still lets you chain further real commands after it, because chaining is about the queue, not a return value.

docs.text: Add a second custom command, cy.addTodo(text), wrapping this course's real todo-add flow (cy.get("#new-todo").type(text) then cy.get("#add-btn").click()), and rewrite the Level 1 todo test to use it. Then deliberately rename #add-btn in todos.html and confirm, by actually running the suite, that only the command definition needs a fix — directly reproducing this lesson's real result on a second, independent real workflow.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real 4-case JSON fixture file, loaded with cy.fixture() and iterated to drive the same login flow with different real data — the same data-driven approach this network's own Selenium course used with plain JSON files, now via Cypress's own built-in fixture loading.

[
  { "name": "valid credentials", "username": "realuser", "password": "realpass123", "expected": "Login Successful" },
  { "name": "wrong password", "username": "realuser", "password": "wrongpass", "expected": "Login Failed" },
  { "name": "wrong username", "username": "wronguser", "password": "realpass123", "expected": "Login Failed" },
  { "name": "empty credentials", "username": "", "password": "", "expected": "Login Failed" }
]

cy.fixture("login-cases.json").then((cases) => {
  expect(cases.length).to.eq(4);
  cases.forEach((c) => {
    cy.visit("/login.html");
    cy.get("#username").type(c.username);
    cy.get("#password").type(c.password);
    cy.get("#submit-btn").click();
    cy.get("#result").should("have.text", c.expected);
  });
});

docs.title: A real bug, caught on the very first run
docs.text:
CypressError: `cy.type()` cannot accept an empty string. You need to actually type something.

The "empty credentials" case's username: "" genuinely crashed the test — not because the login logic is broken, but because .type("") is a real, deliberate Cypress restriction: typing nothing isn't a meaningful user action, so Cypress refuses it outright rather than silently doing nothing. The real fix was to skip the .type() call entirely when the fixture value is empty (the input already starts empty, so there's nothing to type):

if (c.username) cy.get("#username").type(c.username);
if (c.password) cy.get("#password").type(c.password);

✓ loads the real fixture file and iterates its real cases (1265ms)
1 passing (1s)

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: cy.fixture() reads a real file from cypress/fixtures/ and returns its parsed contents (JSON is parsed automatically; other file types come back as text or base64) — it's a real file read, not a mocked or in-memory data structure, which is why the fixture file genuinely needs to exist at that real path. Once loaded, fixture data is just a normal JavaScript value — the .forEach() loop driving four separate real login attempts isn't a Cypress-specific looping construct, it's ordinary JS iterating over real data that happened to come from cy.fixture(). This lesson's real .type("") crash is a deliberate Cypress design choice (not a fixture-specific bug) that exists specifically to catch tests that pass genuinely malformed or empty data without the test author noticing — in this case, correctly flagging that "empty string" needs different handling than "type this string," rather than silently treating them the same way.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming fixture data can always be passed straight into .type() without checking for empty values — this lesson's real crash is exactly what happens when a data-driven test's fixture includes an edge case (empty input) that needs different handling, not identical handling, to the normal cases.
  • Hardcoding fixture file paths with a leading cypress/fixtures/ — cy.fixture("login-cases.json") already resolves relative to that real directory; adding the prefix looks for a nonexistent nested path.
  • Loading a fixture inside every single it() block when the data doesn't change between tests — this lesson's single cy.fixture().then() call loads the real file once and iterates all 4 real cases inside it, which is both faster and avoids 4 separate real file reads for identical data.

docs.title: Exercise
