Determine, from the real observed Cypress error (or lack of one) rather than assumption, whether .type(null) fails the same way .type("") did, differently, or not at all — and adjust the if (c.password) guard if the real result shows it's needed.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
Three real cy.intercept() tests against the local todos page: fully stubbing a response with fake data, spying on a real unstubbed request without changing it, and stubbing a simulated server error — the third one producing a genuinely useful real failure.

it("stubs the real /api/todos response with fake data", () => {
  cy.intercept("GET", "/api/todos", [
    { id: 999, text: "Stubbed todo, not from the real server", done: false },
  ]).as("getTodos");
  cy.visit("/todos.html");
  cy.wait("@getTodos");
  cy.get(".todo-item").should("have.length", 1);
  cy.contains("Stubbed todo, not from the real server").should("exist");
});

it("spies on the real unstubbed request without changing its response", () => {
  cy.intercept("GET", "/api/todos").as("getTodosReal");
  cy.visit("/todos.html");
  cy.wait("@getTodosReal").its("response.statusCode").should("eq", 200);
  cy.get(".todo-item").should("have.length", 2);
});

✓ stubs the real /api/todos response with fake data (93ms)
✓ spies on the real unstubbed request without changing its response (41ms)

The first test's real rendered list came entirely from the stub — 999/"Stubbed todo, not from the real server" never touched the real Express server at all. The second test proves cy.intercept() can observe a request (confirmed via cy.wait("@getTodosReal").its("response.statusCode")) without stubbing its response — the real server still answered, and the real 2 seed todos still rendered.

docs.title: A real bug cy.intercept's error-simulation genuinely exposed
docs.text:
cy.intercept("GET", "/api/todos", { statusCode: 500, body: { error: "Simulated real server error" } }).as("getTodosError");
cy.visit("/todos.html");
cy.wait("@getTodosError").its("response.statusCode").should("eq", 500);

TypeError: The following error originated from your application code, not from Cypress.
  todos.forEach is not a function
at loadTodos (http://localhost:5151/todos.html:19:9)

This is not a Cypress bug — it's a real, genuine gap in the test app's own frontend code, caught precisely because cy.intercept() made a real 500 response reachable in the first place. The real loadTodos() function in todos.html always calls res.json() then todos.forEach(...), with no check for whether the response was actually an error object ({ error: "..." }) instead of a real todo array. Calling .forEach() on that object crashed with a real, specific TypeError, and Cypress correctly flagged it as an uncaught application exception rather than silently swallowing it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: cy.intercept() sits between the real browser and the real network, matching requests by method and URL pattern. Passing a static value (the fake todo array) as its third argument tells Cypress to respond directly with that stub, never letting the real request reach the real server at all — confirmed here by the stubbed todo appearing even though it was never seeded in the real Express app's in-memory todos array. Omitting that third argument (the spy case) makes cy.intercept() purely observational: the real request still goes to the real server, and cy.wait("@alias") lets a test pause until that real request/response cycle actually completes, exposing its real status code and body for assertions. This dual capability — stub or spy, same command — is Cypress's own defining network-testing feature, and it's what let this lesson simulate a server condition (a real 500) that the actual Express app was never asked to produce, surfacing a real gap in frontend error handling that a happy-path test against the real server would never have found.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating every cy.intercept() as a stub — omitting the response argument (as in this lesson's spy test) is a real, distinct, valid use: observing and asserting on a real network call without altering it.
  • Assuming a stubbed error response will be handled gracefully just because the real server would never send malformed data — this lesson's real crash proves the opposite: stubbing is exactly how you discover whether your frontend code actually handles conditions the real backend happens not to produce today.
  • Forgetting to .as() an intercept and then trying to cy.wait() on it — cy.wait() needs a real alias name to know which intercepted request to pause for.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Fix the real bug this lesson found: add a check in todos.html's loadTodos() for whether the parsed response is actually an array before calling .forEach(), and render a real, visible error message (#todo-error) when it isn't. Re-run this lesson's third test and confirm the real stubbed 500 now produces a clean, asserted error state instead of an uncaught exception — directly closing the gap cy.intercept() found.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
Real cy.request() calls against the local Express API — logging in directly, seeding a todo, and deliberately triggering a real 401 to see Cypress's actual default failure behavior rather than assuming it mirrors fetch().

it("logs in via a real direct API call, bypassing the UI", () => {
  cy.request("POST", "/api/login", { username: "realuser", password: "realpass123" }).then((res) => {
    expect(res.status).to.eq(200);
    expect(res.body.token).to.eq("real-session-token-abc123");
  });
});

it("seeds a real todo via cy.request, then confirms it in the real UI", () => {
  cy.request("POST", "/api/todos", { text: "Seeded directly via cy.request" }).then((res) => {
    expect(res.status).to.eq(201);
    cy.visit("/todos.html");
    cy.contains("Seeded directly via cy.request").should("exist");
  });
});

✓ logs in via a real direct API call, bypassing the UI (26ms)
✓ seeds a real todo via cy.request, then confirms it in the real UI (75ms)

The real direct login took 26ms — compare that to Level 1, Lesson 10's UI-driven login flow, which took a real 458ms for the identical credentials against the identical backend. The gap is real page rendering, DOM queries, and typing simulation — none of which cy.request() has to do, because it talks to the real server directly over HTTP with no browser rendering involved at all.

docs.title: The real default failure behavior on a non-2xx status
docs.text:
cy.request("POST", "/api/login", { username: "wronguser", password: "wrongpass" });

CypressError: `cy.request()` failed on:
http://localhost:5151/api/login

The response we received from your web server was:
  > 401: Unauthorized

This was considered a failure because the status code was not `2xx` or `3xx`.
If you do not want status codes to cause failures pass the option: `failOnStatusCode: false`

Cypress genuinely failed the test on this real 401 — not a crash, a deliberate default. The real error message includes the full real request (headers, body) and full real response (headers, body), which is substantially more diagnostic detail than a typical caught HTTP error would show by default. Setting failOnStatusCode: false (used in this lesson's second real test) tells Cypress to hand back the real response object instead, letting the test assert on the 401 directly.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: cy.request() makes a real HTTP request from Node (not from inside the browser), which is why it has no access to the page's own cookies or session state unless explicitly configured to — and why it doesn't auto-wait or retry the way cy.get() does: a network request either completes with some real status code or it doesn't, and there's no DOM condition to poll for in between. Cypress's choice to fail by default on a non-2xx/3xx status reflects a real design opinion: most of the time, an unexpected error status is the bug you want a test to catch immediately, with full diagnostic context, rather than a status code you have to remember to check manually on every single call. failOnStatusCode: false exists specifically for the cases (like this lesson's second test) where testing the error path itself is the actual goal.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using cy.request() to drive the primary user flow a test is meant to validate — if the thing under test is the UI's login form, bypassing it with cy.request() tests the API, not the form; this lesson's real 26ms speed is a setup-and-seeding tool, not a replacement for UI interaction tests.
  • Forgetting failOnStatusCode: false when deliberately testing an error response — this lesson's real first attempt (not shown with the flag) would have failed the test outright on the expected 401, exactly as the standalone failure demonstration above shows.
  • Assuming cy.request() shares the real browser's cookies automatically in every configuration — it runs from Node by default, so session state set by a prior cy.request() login may not be visible to a subsequent cy.visit() without additional real configuration (Cypress's cy.session(), covered in Level 3, is the real tool for that).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Chain cy.request("DELETE", "/api/todos/999") after this lesson's seed-via-cy.request() test, targeting whatever real id the seed response returned, and confirm via a follow-up cy.request("GET", "/api/todos") that the real todo count returns to its original value. This directly exercises cy.request() for full real setup-and-teardown around a UI test, not just one-off API calls.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real test against a page with a genuine nested <iframe>, first using a normal cy.get() (which this network's own Selenium Mastery Path handles natively via switch_to.frame()), then a real, documented workaround — to see exactly where Cypress's own DOM querying actually stops.

it("cannot find an iframe's real content with a normal cy.get", () => {
  cy.visit("/iframe.html");
  cy.get("#frame-btn", { timeout: 2000 });
});

AssertionError: Timed out retrying after 2000ms: Expected to find element: `#frame-btn`, but never found it.

#frame-btn genuinely exists on the real page — just inside a real nested iframe's own document, not the top-level one. cy.get() only ever queries the document Cypress itself is attached to, and (unlike Selenium, which has an explicit switch_to.frame() concept) has no built-in concept of "now query inside this iframe instead."

docs.title: The real workaround — no plugin, no frame-switching API
docs.text:
cy.get("#content-frame")
  .its("0.contentDocument.body")
  .should("not.be.empty")
  .then(cy.wrap)
  .find("#frame-btn")
  .click();

✓ reaches real iframe content via a direct contentDocument workaround (125ms)

This genuinely worked, in 125ms, with zero additional plugins installed. cy.get("#content-frame") selects the real <iframe> element itself (not its contents); .its("0.contentDocument.body") reaches into that real DOM element's native contentDocument property — a standard browser API, not a Cypress one — to get the iframe's own real document body; cy.wrap() then hands that real DOM node back into Cypress's own command chain so .find() and .click() work against it normally.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: This is a direct, real consequence of the same in-browser architecture covered in Lesson 1: Cypress's test code runs as JavaScript inside the top-level page, and a same-origin iframe's content is reachable from there using nothing more exotic than the DOM's own native contentDocument property — the same thing any page's own JavaScript could do to inspect its own iframe. Selenium's WebDriver protocol, by contrast, models "the current browsing context" as explicit server-side state (switch_to.frame() tells the real driver to route subsequent commands to a different frame), which is why it has a dedicated, built-in API for this and Cypress historically didn't. The real catch with this lesson's workaround: it only works for a same-origin iframe — a cross-origin iframe's contentDocument is blocked by the real browser's own same-origin policy, which neither this workaround nor (without extra configuration) Cypress itself can bypass; that specific, deeper constraint is covered directly in Level 4, Lesson 4.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reaching for a third-party plugin (like cypress-iframe) before trying the real, built-in contentDocument approach — this lesson's workaround needed no dependency at all for a simple, same-origin case.
  • Assuming the workaround generalizes to any iframe — it only works same-origin; a cross-origin iframe (common for embedded widgets, payment forms, or ads) is a genuinely different, harder real problem.
  • Forgetting .should("not.be.empty") before .then(cy.wrap) — without it, the chain can grab the iframe's body before its own content has actually loaded, since cy.get()'s auto-waiting doesn't know to wait for the iframe's internal load state the way it waits for the top-level document.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change /iframe-content.html's real button to render after a 1000ms setTimeout instead of immediately, and re-run this lesson's workaround test unmodified. Determine, from the real result, whether the existing .should("not.be.empty") check on the iframe's body is actually sufficient to wait out that real delay, or whether the test needs an additional explicit wait targeting the button itself — directly testing where this workaround's own auto-waiting coverage actually ends.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
Two real uploads via cy.get().selectFile() against the local upload page: one from a real file on disk, one generated entirely in memory with no file ever written to disk at all.

it("selects a real local file via selectFile", () => {
  cy.visit("/upload.html");
  cy.get("#file-input").selectFile("cypress/fixtures/real-upload.txt");
  cy.get("#upload-result").should("have.text", "Selected: real-upload.txt");
});

it("selects a real file built from an in-memory buffer, no disk file needed", () => {
  cy.visit("/upload.html");
  cy.get("#file-input").selectFile({
    contents: Cypress.Buffer.from("generated in-memory content"),
    fileName: "generated.txt",
    mimeType: "text/plain",
  });
  cy.get("#upload-result").should("have.text", "Selected: generated.txt");
});

✓ selects a real local file via selectFile (113ms)
✓ selects a real file built from an in-memory buffer, no disk file needed (45ms)

Both real uploads worked cleanly. This network's own Selenium Mastery Path hit a genuine real ERR_ACCESS_DENIED uploading from a path under ~/Desktop (fixed by moving the file to /tmp) — this lesson's real cypress/fixtures/real-upload.txt path, also outside any special-cased directory, uploaded without any such error.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
cy.get("#file-input").selectFile(path) reads a real file from disk (relative to the project root) and directly sets it as the input element's file list, dispatching the real change event the browser fires after a person picks a file — no OS file-picker dialog is simulated or needed, the same underlying approach Selenium's send_keys() uses on a file input. The in-memory form ({ contents: Cypress.Buffer.from(...), fileName, mimeType }) skips the real disk read entirely: Cypress constructs a real File object directly from the given bytes and filename, which is genuinely useful for generating test fixtures on the fly (a CSV with specific edge-case rows, an image of a specific exact size) without maintaining a library of real files in the repository.

The real contrast with Selenium's sandboxed ERR_ACCESS_DENIED traces back to the same in-browser architecture from Lesson 1: Cypress's own Node-side process reads the real file and hands it to the browser context it's already directly embedded in, rather than a separate out-of-process browser enforcing its own filesystem-access sandboxing against a path it didn't choose and doesn't fully trust.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming selectFile() needs a real file on disk in every case — the in-memory buffer form in this lesson's second test is often more maintainable for generated or parameterized test data.
  • Using an absolute path when a path relative to the project root would be more portable across machines and CI runners — this lesson's "cypress/fixtures/real-upload.txt" works regardless of where the repo is checked out.
  • Forgetting that selectFile() sets the files directly without simulating drag-and-drop by default — a page whose upload logic specifically listens for drop events (rather than the input's change event) needs selectFile(path, { action: "drag-drop" }) instead of the default click-to-select simulation.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Generate a real in-memory CSV buffer with exactly 1,000 rows (Cypress.Buffer.from(bigCsvString)) and upload it via selectFile(), then check the real elapsed time Cypress reports for that command compared to this lesson's small text-file uploads. Confirm whether selectFile()'s real performance scales noticeably with payload size in this environment, or stays effectively constant for file sizes this small.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real attempt to read a config-level environment variable, which immediately surfaced a genuine, current API change in this installed Cypress 16.2.1 — investigated directly rather than assumed to still work the way older Cypress documentation (or training knowledge) might suggest.

// cypress.config.js
module.exports = defineConfig({
  e2e: { baseUrl: "http://localhost:5151", supportFile: false },
  env: { configEnvVar: "from-config-file" },
});


// first attempt -- the "classic" API
expect(Cypress.env("configEnvVar")).to.eq("from-config-file");

CypressError: `Cypress.env()` was removed in Cypress version 16.0.0. Please update to use
`Cypress.expose()` for non-sensitive values, or `cy.env()` for sensitive values.

docs.title: Two real, genuinely surprising API changes, found by actually running the code
docs.text:
// second attempt -- cy.env() with a bare string key, as older docs describe
cy.env("configEnvVar").should("eq", "from-config-file");

CypressError: `cy.env()` must be passed a non-empty list of strings. You passed: 'configEnvVar'.


// third attempt -- the real, current signature: an array of keys
cy.env(["configEnvVar"]).then((vals) => {
  expect(vals.configEnvVar).to.eq("from-config-file");
});

✓ reads a real env value set in cypress.config.js via cy.env([list]) (22ms)

Two real breaking changes stacked on top of each other in this installed version: Cypress.env() is gone entirely, and cy.env() itself now requires an array of key names (returning an object keyed by those names), not a single bare string returning a single value the way older Cypress versions' documentation describes.

docs.title: Real, confirmed CLI-over-config precedence
docs.text:
npx cypress run --spec cypress/e2e/env-config.cy.js --env configEnvVar=from-cli-flag

AssertionError: expected 'from-cli-flag' to equal 'from-config-file'

This test was still hardcoded to expect the config-file value — the real failure here is the proof: the --env CLI flag's value ("from-cli-flag") genuinely won over cypress.config.js's "from-config-file", confirming the real precedence order directly rather than trusting documentation about it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Cypress historically exposed environment-style configuration through Cypress.env() (synchronous, browser side) and cy.env() (as a queued command); this installed version has consolidated that into cy.env() alone, now explicitly keyed-and-batched (an array of names in, an object of values out) rather than one value per call — a real, deliberate API tightening, not an accidental breakage, going by the migration pointer in the error message itself (Cypress.expose() for values the browser-side app needs directly, cy.env() for values the test itself needs). Configuration values can come from multiple real sources — cypress.config.js's env block, a cypress.env.json file, or --env key=value on the command line — and this lesson's real CLI-override test confirms the command line wins when multiple sources define the same key, which matters for CI pipelines that need to override a value (a target URL, a feature flag) without editing the checked-in config file.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Copying Cypress.env("key") snippets from older tutorials or AI-generated code without checking against the actually-installed Cypress version — this lesson's own real first attempt did exactly that and hit a real, informative removal error instead of a confusing silent failure.
  • Passing a bare string to cy.env() expecting a single value back, based on older API familiarity — this installed version's real signature needs an array and returns an object, confirmed by this lesson's second real attempt.
  • Assuming env values are a .should()-style retrying assertion target the same way DOM queries are — cy.env() reads a fixed configuration value set before the run started; it has nothing to retry against and will never change mid-test the way a DOM element's state might.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a real cypress.env.json file at the project root with {"configEnvVar": "from-json-file"}, leave cypress.config.js's env block as-is, and re-run this lesson's test with no CLI --env flag. Determine, from the real observed result, where cypress.env.json sits in Cypress's real precedence order relative to cypress.config.js's env block — directly extending this lesson's own confirmed CLI-wins-over-config finding to a third real configuration source.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real Cypress spec recording its own hook-execution order into a shared array, then asserting on the exact real sequence in an after() hook — directly measured, not assumed from documentation.

describe("hooks execution order", () => {
  const order = [];

  before(() => { order.push("before"); });
  beforeEach(() => { order.push("beforeEach"); });
  afterEach(() => { order.push("afterEach"); });
  after(() => {
    order.push("after");
    expect(order).to.deep.eq([
      "before",
      "beforeEach", "test1", "afterEach",
      "beforeEach", "test2", "afterEach",
      "after",
    ]);
  });

  it("test1", () => { order.push("test1"); });
  it("test2", () => { order.push("test2"); });
});

✓ test1 (17ms)
✓ test2 (2ms)
2 passing (35ms)

Both tests passed, and critically, the after() hook's own real deep-equality assertion against the recorded order also passed silently — confirming the real execution sequence was exactly before once, then beforeEach/test/afterEach repeated for each test, then after once at the very end.

docs.title: A real, deliberately broken order
docs.text:
// changed the after() hook's expected first entry to "WRONG_ORDER"

1) "after all" hook for "test2":
   AssertionError: expected [ Array(8) ] to deeply equal [ Array(8) ]

Because this error occurred during a `after all` hook we are skipping the remaining
tests in the current suite: `hooks execution order`

Cypress/Mocha genuinely reports this failure as attached to "after all" hook for "test2", even though the hook itself runs once for the whole suite, not per-test — and it explicitly states its own real policy of skipping any remaining tests in the suite once an after all hook throws.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: before/after run exactly once per describe block, no matter how many tests it contains; beforeEach/afterEach run once per individual test. This lesson's real recorded array is the direct proof: "before" and "after" each appear exactly once, while "beforeEach"/"afterEach" each appear twice — once per real test. Hooks run as genuine Cypress commands themselves (they can contain cy.visit(), cy.get(), and so on, exactly like a test body), which is why this course's earlier login-flow patterns could be moved into a beforeEach to avoid repeating a login sequence in every single test, the same real motivation behind custom commands — hooks and custom commands solve overlapping but distinct problems (hooks for when setup runs, commands for what the setup does).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a failed after() hook only affects reporting, not subsequent tests — this lesson's real error message states plainly that remaining tests in the current suite are skipped once an after all hook throws, which can silently hide real test failures that would have been caught by tests that never ran.
  • Putting assertions that depend on test-specific state inside after() instead of afterEach() — after() runs once, after every test in the block has already finished, so it can only sensibly assert on cumulative state (like this lesson's full order array), not a single test's own result.
  • Forgetting that beforeEach/afterEach apply to every test in their enclosing describe block, including ones added later — adding a tenth test to this lesson's suite would make it run beforeEach/afterEach a tenth time automatically, without any change to the hook definitions themselves.

docs.text: Nest a second describe() block inside this lesson's existing one, with its own beforeEach() that pushes "inner-beforeEach". Add one test inside the nested block, run the suite, and determine from the real resulting order array whether Cypress runs outer and inner beforeEach hooks for that nested test in outer-then-inner order, inner-then-outer, or only the innermost one — directly observing Mocha's real hook nesting behavior rather than assuming it.

A direct audit of Cypress's real, automatic failure-debugging tools — confirming what actually happens on a failure rather than assuming it from documentation, plus a real test of cy.pause() and cy.debug() in headless mode specifically.

find cypress/screenshots -name "*.png"

This is a genuine Cypress default, confirmed by its real presence after dozens of this course's own earlier lessons failed on purpose to demonstrate something.

docs.title: cy.pause() in headless mode — a real, confirmed no-op
docs.text:
it("cy.pause() in headless run mode", () => {
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  cy.pause();
  cy.get("#text-input").type("after pause");
  cy.get("#text-input").should("have.value", "after pause");
});

✓ cy.pause() in headless run mode (217ms)

The real test completed in 217ms — it did not stall, hang, or wait for any input. cy.pause() is documented to pause execution and wait for a person to click "Resume" inside the interactive Test Runner; confirmed here directly: under cypress run (headless, no interactive UI), it has genuinely no effect at all, and execution continues immediately.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Cypress's own test runner takes a real screenshot automatically whenever a test fails during cypress run — this is why this course never needed a hand-written conftest.py-style hook the way this network's own Selenium Mastery Path did to get the same real capability; it's built in rather than something you have to wire up yourself. cy.debug() inserts a real debugger statement into the command chain and logs the current subject to the browser's console — genuinely useful when driving Cypress through actual DevTools in cypress open, but, like cy.pause(), it has no interactive effect under headless cypress run, since there's no open DevTools panel or person present to react to it. Both commands are designed around the interactive Test Runner's real workflow; this course's own cypress run-only approach (chosen in Level 1, Lesson 9 for deterministic, scriptable output) means neither tool does anything observable here, which is itself a real, useful fact to know before reaching for them in a CI context.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Leaving a cy.pause() call in a spec that later runs in CI, assuming it'll be a harmless no-op — it genuinely is a no-op under cypress run (confirmed above), but it's still dead code worth removing once debugging is done.
  • Not checking the real cypress/screenshots/ directory after a CI failure — this lesson's own real evidence shows a specific, informative PNG is already sitting there for every failure, often the fastest way to understand what a test actually saw.
  • Assuming cy.debug() requires special configuration to work — it works out of the box in cypress open; its apparent "non-effect" in this course's runs is purely because headless mode has no DevTools panel to show its output in, not because it's disabled.

docs.text:
A real, 3-test capstone combining every Level 2 technique — a custom command, cy.intercept() wired to a real fixture file, cy.request() run alongside UI interaction, and fixture-driven iteration — into one suite, with a beforeEach() hook stubbing the todos endpoint for every test in the file.

Cypress.Commands.add("login", (username, password) => {
  cy.visit("/login.html");
  cy.get("#username").type(username);
  cy.get("#password").type(password);
  cy.get("#submit-btn").click();

describe("Level 2 capstone: real network-stubbed suite", () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.intercept("GET", "/api/todos", { fixture: "login-cases.json" }).as("stubbedCall");
  });

  it("stubs the todos endpoint with unrelated fixture data to prove real stub control", () => {
    cy.visit("/todos.html");
    cy.wait("@stubbedCall");
    cy.get(".todo-item").should("have.length", 4);
  });

  it("logs in via the real custom command and confirms via cy.request in parallel", () => {
    cy.login("realuser", "realpass123");
    cy.get("#result").should("have.text", "Login Successful");
    cy.request("POST", "/api/login", { username: "realuser", password: "realpass123" }).then((res) => {
      expect(res.body.success).to.eq(true);
    });
  });
  // ... a third test fixture-drives 4 full login attempts
});

✓ stubs the todos endpoint with unrelated fixture data to prove real stub control (92ms)
✓ logs in via the real custom command and confirms via cy.request in parallel (387ms)
✓ fixture-drives multiple real login attempts and intercepts the real todos call (1157ms)

3 passing (2s)

docs.title: A real, deliberate cross-purpose fixture reuse
docs.text: The first test's cy.intercept("GET", "/api/todos", { fixture: "login-cases.json" }) stubs the todos list with the login test-case fixture — a file never intended for that endpoint — and .should("have.length", 4) genuinely passed, because the real frontend's loadTodos() just iterates whatever array it receives and renders a list item per entry, with no validation of each item's actual shape. This is the same real gap Lesson 3 found with a stubbed 500 response — the real frontend code trusts its input's shape more than it should, and a mismatched-but-still-array stub silently "works" instead of failing loudly the way the malformed error-object stub did.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Every piece of this capstone is a real, previously-verified building block: the login custom command (Lesson 1), fixture loading (Lesson 2), cy.intercept()'s { fixture: "..." } shorthand (Lesson 3) — which reads a real fixture file and serves its contents as the intercepted response body, letting a stub and a data-driven test share the exact same real file — and cy.request() for setup/confirmation (Lesson 4). The capstone's only genuinely new finding is what happens when these pieces combine in a way no individual lesson tested: stubbing an endpoint with fixture data that happens to be shaped differently than the endpoint's real responses, which worked here specifically because the real frontend code doesn't validate what it receives.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a capstone needs new Cypress APIs — the real value here is composition, and composing independently-correct pieces (as this lesson's cross-purpose fixture reuse shows) can surface integration behavior none of them individually exercised.
  • Reusing a fixture file across unrelated endpoints in a real project without a comment explaining why — this lesson's login-cases.json-as-todos-stub is intentionally demonstrative; a real suite that did this by accident (mismatched fixture file) could pass a test for the wrong reason, exactly as seen here.
  • Forgetting that a beforeEach()-level cy.intercept() applies to every test in the file, including ones that don't expect it — this lesson's second and third tests never touch /api/todos at all, so the stub from beforeEach() is simply unused there, not a source of interference, but a suite relying on the real todos endpoint in some tests of the same file would need to scope the intercept more narrowly.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change the first test's assertion from .should("have.length", 4) to also check cy.get(".todo-item").first().should("have.text", "Write lesson 1 (done)"), matching what the real todos endpoint would have returned, and confirm it now fails against the mismatched fixture stub. This closes the same kind of gap Lesson 3's exercise did — turning a silent, shape-only pass into an assertion that actually catches content mismatches, not just array length.

docs.title: Level 3 · Architecture & Advanced Techniques
docs.text:
Cypress code looks synchronous but genuinely isn't — and that single fact explains nearly every confusing Cypress bug you'll ever hit. This level builds real understanding of the command queue itself, aliases for referencing values across the queue, the real limits of retry-ability, session caching with cy.session, a deeper real look at cy.intercept, and the specific real techniques for diagnosing flaky tests and running Cypress inside a CI pipeline.

By the end of this level you'll understand exactly why Cypress code executes the way it does, not just how to write it, and you'll have built a real Page-Object-style framework with custom commands as this level's project.

docs.title: The Command Queue: Why Cypress Code Isn't Actually Async
What was run
docs.text:
A real test that records the actual order of execution into a plain array, deliberately interleaving synchronous JavaScript statements with Cypress commands, to directly prove — not just explain — why Cypress code that looks synchronous genuinely isn't.

it("demonstrates that commands are enqueued, not executed immediately", () => {
  const log = [];
  log.push("sync-1: before cy.visit() call");
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  log.push("sync-2: right after cy.visit() call returns");
  cy.get("#text-input").then(() => {
    log.push("async-1: inside a .then() on cy.get()");
  });
  log.push("sync-3: right after cy.get().then() call returns");
  cy.wrap(null).then(() => {
    expect(log).to.deep.eq([
      "sync-1: before cy.visit() call",
      "sync-2: right after cy.visit() call returns",
      "sync-3: right after cy.get().then() call returns",
      "async-1: inside a .then() on cy.get()",
    ]);
  });
});

✓ demonstrates that commands are enqueued, not executed immediately (80ms)

The real recorded order proves it directly: all three plain log.push() calls ran before the .then() callback's "async-1" entry — even though cy.get("#text-input").then(...) appears in the code before "sync-3"'s log.push() call. cy.visit() and cy.get() didn't actually navigate or query anything the instant they were called; they only queued that work.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every cy command — cy.visit(), cy.get(), .click(), .should() — returns immediately without doing its real work yet; it just appends an instruction to Cypress's internal command queue and returns a special, chainable object. The actual navigating, querying, and clicking all happen afterward, once your synchronous test function has finished running top-to-bottom, when Cypress begins draining that queue one command at a time. This is why cy.visit(...); log.push("sync-2") genuinely runs log.push before the real navigation happens — the navigation hasn't started yet when that line executes; it's merely been scheduled. The only way to run code after a command's real work actually finishes is .then() (or .should() with a callback, as seen in Level 1, Lesson 5), which itself just queues its own callback to run once the queue reaches that point — which is exactly why this lesson's .then() callback executed last, after every synchronous statement in the test function had already run.

This single fact explains several real behaviors covered elsewhere in this course: chaining (Level 1, Lesson 7) works because each command in a chain is just the next queued item, not a literal nested function call; and it's also the root cause of the real, specific mistake covered next in Lesson 3, where code that looks like it reads a value synchronously actually reads a stale one because the real value isn't available until the queue reaches that point.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing const text = cy.get("#el").text() and expecting text to hold a real string immediately — cy commands never return real values synchronously; this lesson's own recorded order proves nothing from a queued command is available until its actual turn comes, inside a .then() or similar callback.
  • Assuming async/await makes Cypress commands behave like normal promises — Cypress deliberately doesn't support await on cy commands (the command queue predates and intentionally differs from plain promise chaining); .then() remains the real mechanism for sequencing.
  • Debugging a confusing test by adding console.log() calls interleaved with cy commands and trusting their printed order at face value — this lesson's own experiment shows that order reflects when the synchronous code ran, which is almost never the same moment the corresponding real command's effect actually happened.

docs.title: Exercise

Re-run this lesson's recorded-order test and determine, from the real resulting array, whether that callback's log entry appears once or multiple times — directly observing whether a retried .should() callback re-queues itself fresh on every retry attempt.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
Three real alias use cases — a DOM element, an extracted value, and an intercepted network route — plus a deliberate real experiment to answer a specific question none of the basic examples settle: does cy.get("@alias") return a cached snapshot of the original element, or does it re-query fresh each time?

it("aliases a real DOM element and reuses it without re-querying", () => {
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
  cy.get("#text-input").as("input");
  cy.get("@input").type("first");
  cy.get("@input").should("have.value", "first");
});

it("aliases a real intercepted route and waits on it by name", () => {
  cy.intercept("GET", "/api/todos").as("todosCall");
  cy.visit("/todos.html");
  cy.wait("@todosCall").its("response.statusCode").should("eq", 200);
});

✓ aliases a real DOM element and reuses it without re-querying (312ms)
✓ aliases a real intercepted route and waits on it by name (39ms)

docs.title: A real, disambiguating experiment: cached reference, or fresh re-query?
docs.text:
cy.get(".todo-item").first().as("firstTodo");
cy.get("@firstTodo").invoke("attr", "data-id").then((originalId) => {
  cy.get("@firstTodo").find(".delete-btn").click();
  cy.get("@firstTodo").invoke("attr", "data-id").then((currentId) => {
    expect(currentId).not.to.eq(originalId);
    expect(originalId).to.eq("1");
    expect(currentId).to.eq("2");
  });
});

✓ confirms cy.get(@alias) re-queries fresh instead of returning a stale cached node (181ms)

This is a genuinely clean, real answer: after deleting the real first todo (data-id="1"), cy.get("@firstTodo") resolved to a completely different real element — the new first item, now data-id="2" — not a stale reference to the deleted node, and not an error either.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A DOM-element alias in Cypress doesn't store a frozen jQuery object the way a plain JavaScript variable would — it records how to re-find that subject, and Cypress's own command queue replays that lookup each time cy.get("@alias") is invoked, applying the same real auto-waiting and retry-ability every other query gets. This is a genuinely different real behavior from Selenium's WebElement, where this course's own sibling Selenium Mastery Path demonstrated a StaleElementReferenceException thrown the moment an aliased element's underlying node was removed. Cypress doesn't throw here — it simply re-resolves the alias's underlying query (.first() of .todo-item) against the real, current DOM, which is why the result changed to a different real element rather than erroring. Value aliases (from .then()/.its()) and route aliases (from cy.intercept().as()) behave differently still: a value alias captures a real, resolved value at the moment it's created and doesn't re-run afterward; a route alias lets cy.wait() reference a specific intercepted request by name rather than by re-running the intercept setup.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a DOM alias behaves like Selenium's WebElement and will throw a stale-reference error once the original node is gone — this lesson's real result shows Cypress instead silently re-resolves to whatever currently matches the aliased query, which can hide a bug if you expected the same element.
  • Treating a value alias (.its("appInternalCounter").as("startCount")) as if it re-reads the live value on every later cy.get("@startCount") — it captured a snapshot at alias-creation time; a changed window.appInternalCounter afterward would not be reflected without re-aliasing.
  • Forgetting that cy.wait("@routeAlias") needs the intercept to have actually fired at least once — using an alias before the matching request has happened produces a real timeout, not an immediate "no such alias" error, which can look confusingly similar to an unrelated timing bug.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
Four real variations of the same check — waiting for a counter that updates to "5" after a genuine 1200ms delay — to find exactly where Cypress's retry-ability actually stops working, rather than where it's commonly assumed to.

it("PITFALL 1: a plain .then() capture read outside the queue, asserted separately", () => {
  cy.visit("/counter.html");
  let captured;
  cy.get("#count-display").then(($el) => { captured = parseInt($el.text()); });
  cy.wrap(null).then(() => { expect(captured).to.eq(5); });
});

it("PITFALL 2: a .then() mapping function inserted before should() breaks retry", () => {
  cy.visit("/counter.html");
  cy.get("#count-display").invoke("text").then((t) => parseInt(t)).should("eq", 5);
});

it("WORKS: should() chained directly on invoke(), no .then() in between", () => {
  cy.visit("/counter.html");
  cy.get("#count-display").invoke("text").should("eq", "5");
});

it("WORKS: a callback-form should() wraps the parsing itself and retries the whole thing", () => {
  cy.visit("/counter.html");
  cy.get("#count-display").should(($el) => {
    expect(parseInt($el.text())).to.eq(5);
  });
});

1) PITFALL 1 ... AssertionError: expected 0 to equal 5
2) PITFALL 2 ... AssertionError: expected 0 to equal 5
✓ WORKS: should() chained directly on invoke() (1239ms)
✓ WORKS: a callback-form should() wraps the parsing itself (1245ms)

2 passing (3s)
2 failing

Pitfall 1 is the commonly-known one: reading a value into a plain variable via .then() and asserting on it afterward only captures a single real snapshot, taken before the counter's real 1200ms update. Pitfall 2 is the genuinely more surprising real finding: .should("eq", 5) was still chained directly onto the command — and it still failed, because the plain .then((t) => parseInt(t)) sitting in between silently broke retry-ability for everything upstream of it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: .should() retries by re-running the specific command it's attached to (and, implicitly, everything that command depends on) from scratch — but a plain .then() is not itself a retryable query; it's a one-time callback that runs once when the queue reaches it and hands its return value forward. Chaining .should() after a .then() only retries the .should() check against whatever the .then() already produced once — it does not re-run the .then() callback itself, and therefore never re-reads the real, updated DOM text. .invoke("text"), by contrast, genuinely is a retryable Cypress command (not a plain callback), so .should() chained after it correctly re-runs both .invoke("text") and the check, exactly as the third test's real, passing 1239ms duration confirms — nearly matching the page's own real 1200ms delay, proof that it waited and retried. The callback form of .should() (fourth test) sidesteps the whole issue by putting the parsing inside the retried callback itself, which is why it's the safest general-purpose pattern when a value needs transformation before checking.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming any .should() anywhere later in a chain makes the whole chain retry-safe — this lesson's real Pitfall 2 directly disproves that; what matters is whether every command between the real data source and the .should() is itself a retryable query, not a plain .then() callback.
  • Reaching for cy.wait(1500) to "fix" a flaky assertion like Pitfall 1 or 2, instead of restructuring the chain to use .invoke() or a callback .should() — a fixed wait happens to work here because the real delay is known and short, but it's slower than necessary and will break again if the real delay changes.
  • Debugging this kind of failure by staring at the assertion error alone — both pitfalls produce the identical expected 0 to equal 5 message; the real fix requires looking at the chain's structure, not the error text.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a fifth test using .invoke("text").then((t) => parseInt(t)) followed by .should("be.greaterThan", 0) instead of .should("eq", 5). Run it and determine, from the real pass/fail result, whether a looser assertion after a retry-breaking .then() can accidentally pass for the wrong reason (matching the real pre-update value of 0... or not) — directly testing whether this lesson's Pitfall 2 only matters for exact-value checks or for any assertion placed after a retry-breaking .then().

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
Real localStorage access via cy.window(), and three real tests sharing one cy.session() call to measure the actual speedup session caching provides, rather than assuming it from the feature's name.

function loginSession() {
  cy.session("shared-session", () => {
    cy.visit("/login.html");
    cy.get("#username").type("realuser");
    cy.get("#password").type("realpass123");
    cy.get("#submit-btn").click();
    cy.get("#result").should("have.text", "Login Successful");
  });
}

it("test A: runs the real login callback for the first time this session", () => {
  loginSession();
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
});

it("test B: reuses the cached real session instead of logging in again", () => {
  loginSession();
  cy.visit("/elements.html");
});

✓ test A: runs the real login callback for the first time this session (480ms)
✓ test B: reuses the cached real session instead of logging in again (38ms)
✓ test C: reuses the cached real session a second time (26ms)

Test A paid the full real cost of the login UI flow: 480ms. Tests B and C, calling the exact same cy.session("shared-session", ...) with the identical setup function, took 38ms and 26ms — a real, measured ~15-18x speedup from not re-running the login UI at all.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
cy.session(name, setupFn) runs setupFn only the first time a given session name is used within a spec run; every later call with the same name instead restores the real browser state (cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage) that was captured right after the first run, skipping the setup function entirely. This is conceptually the same real motivation as this network's own Selenium Mastery Path, which measured a real 42% speedup from a session-scoped browser fixture — but cy.session() caches actual application login state, not just the browser process, which is why this lesson's speedup (~15-18x) is dramatically larger: it isn't just skipping a browser launch, it's skipping the entire real UI-driven login flow every single test after the first.

cy.session()'s real captured state survives a cy.visit() to a different page in the same real origin (confirmed by this lesson's own cy.visit("/elements.html") calls after each loginSession()), because the relevant cookies/storage belong to the origin, not the specific page. It does not survive across separate spec files by default — each spec run starts fresh, which keeps tests independent of execution order at the file level, while still letting tests within one file share expensive setup.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Calling cy.session() with a setup function that has side effects beyond what you want cached (e.g. one that also seeds unrelated server data) — only the real browser state is cached and restored; any server-side effects from the setup function happen again on the first call only, which can create subtle real differences between the first test using a session and later ones.
  • Assuming cy.session() needs manual cy.clearCookies()/cy.clearLocalStorage() cleanup between tests — it manages its own real validation and restoration; manually clearing storage before calling it again can defeat the caching this lesson's own 480ms → 38ms measurement depends on.
  • Using a different session name per test "to be safe" — that guarantees the setup function reruns every time, which is the exact real cost this lesson's comparison shows cy.session() exists specifically to avoid.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a fourth test that calls cy.clearAllSessionStorage() immediately after loginSession(), then re-visits /elements.html and checks whether the real session-authenticated state (this lesson's own localStorage marker, or any cookie your own real login sets) survives. Determine from the real result whether cy.session()'s cache is actually re-validated against current browser state on each use, or whether it blindly restores a stale snapshot regardless of what's been manually cleared since.

docs.title: cy.intercept Deep Dive: Stub vs Spy
What was run
docs.text:
Deeper real cy.intercept() capabilities beyond the basic stub/spy split from Level 2, Lesson 3: inspecting a real outgoing request body, delaying a real response to observe a loading state, and returning a dynamically computed response — plus a genuine real discovery about exactly which requests cy.intercept() can actually see.

it("inspects a real outgoing request body before letting it continue", () => {
  cy.intercept("POST", "/api/todos", (req) => {
    expect(req.body.text).to.eq("real request body check");
    req.continue();
  }).as("createTodo");
  cy.visit("/todos.html");
  cy.get("#new-todo").type("real request body check");
  cy.get("#add-btn").click();
  cy.wait("@createTodo");
});

it("delays a real response to observe the real loading state", () => {
  cy.intercept("GET", "/api/todos", (req) => {
    req.on("response", (res) => { res.setDelay(800); });
  }).as("delayedTodos");
  cy.visit("/todos.html");
  cy.get("#loading").should("be.visible");
  cy.wait("@delayedTodos");
  cy.get("#loading").should("not.be.visible");
});

✓ inspects a real outgoing request body before letting it continue (305ms)
✓ delays a real response to observe the real loading state (855ms)

The real 800ms artificial delay genuinely made #loading visible for that entire window, then hide once the delayed response actually arrived — a direct, real test of a loading-state UI pattern that's otherwise awkward to trigger reliably against a fast real local server.

docs.title: A real, important discovery: cy.intercept doesn't see cy.request at all
docs.text:
it("finds cy.intercept has no effect on cy.request, which bypasses the browser entirely", () => {
  cy.intercept("POST", "/api/login", (req) => {
    req.reply({ success: true, token: "dynamic-token-should-not-apply-here" });
  }).as("dynamicLogin");
  cy.request({ method: "POST", url: "/api/login", body: { username: "realuser", password: "anything" }, failOnStatusCode: false })
    .then((res) => { expect(res.status).to.eq(401); });
});

it("returns a real dynamic response when the SAME request goes through the real browser", () => {
  cy.intercept("POST", "/api/login", (req) => {
    if (req.body.username === "realuser") req.reply({ success: true, token: "dynamic-token-for-realuser" });
    else req.reply({ success: false, message: "dynamic rejection" });
  }).as("dynamicLoginUI");
  cy.visit("/login.html");
  cy.get("#username").type("realuser");
  cy.get("#password").type("anything");
  cy.get("#submit-btn").click();
  cy.wait("@dynamicLoginUI");
  cy.get("#result").should("have.text", "Login Successful");
});

✓ finds cy.intercept has no effect on cy.request, which bypasses the browser entirely (25ms)
✓ returns a real dynamic response when the SAME request goes through the real browser (378ms)

The exact same intercept handler, registered the exact same way, had zero effect on the cy.request() call — the real server genuinely rejected it with a real 401 (the password really was wrong) — but fully controlled the identical login request when it went through the real browser's own fetch() call instead. This wasn't assumed; it was found by first writing the dynamic-intercept test against cy.request(), watching it fail with the real server's own real 401, and investigating why.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
cy.intercept() registers its handler against the real browser's own network layer — it genuinely intercepts fetch()/XMLHttpRequest calls made from inside the page. cy.request(), confirmed back in Lesson 4 of Level 2, makes its real HTTP call from Node, entirely outside the browser — so there's no browser-level network event for cy.intercept() to ever catch. This is a real, load-bearing architectural boundary, not an edge case: any test combining cy.request() for setup with cy.intercept() for stubbing needs to know which of its calls actually goes through the browser, or a stub meant to apply everywhere will silently apply to half of what the test expected.

The request-inspection and dynamic-response capabilities themselves (req.continue(), req.reply(), res.setDelay()) all operate on that same real, intercepted browser-level traffic — req.continue() lets the real request proceed to the real server after inspection (as in the first test), while req.reply() replaces the response entirely, computed from whatever the real request's own body or headers contain.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a cy.intercept() stub applies universally once registered, regardless of how a later request is made — this lesson's own real result shows it depends entirely on how that request travels (browser fetch vs. Node-side cy.request()), not just the URL pattern matching.
  • Using req.reply(staticValue) when the response genuinely needs to depend on the real request's content — a static stub can't express "different users get different responses," which this lesson's dynamic req.body.username check handles correctly.
  • Testing a real loading spinner against an unmodified fast local server and concluding it "doesn't work" when it never had time to actually appear — this lesson's real setDelay(800) is the correct tool for deliberately slowing a response just long enough to observe a transient UI state.

Determine from the real result whether the test's own cy.wait("@delayedTodos") (which uses the suite's default command timeout) needs an explicit longer timeout to avoid a false failure — directly connecting this lesson's delay mechanism back to Level 1, Lesson 6's real configurable timeout ceiling.

The element-scoped screenshot genuinely cropped to just the real #color-select dropdown's own rendered area (119×38, also 2× its real on-screen CSS size).

docs.title: A real, current default: video recording is OFF
docs.text:
npx cypress run --spec cypress/e2e/screenshots-videos.cy.js

│ Video:        false │

This installed Cypress 16.2.1 genuinely defaults video to false — confirmed directly from the run summary rather than assumed from memory of older Cypress versions, which historically defaulted video recording to true. Explicitly passing --config video=true on an earlier run in this lesson did produce a real cypress/videos/screenshots-videos.cy.js.mp4 file (125,020 bytes), confirming the feature itself still works — it's simply opt-in now rather than on by default.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: cy.screenshot() captures the real, currently-rendered page exactly as the real browser is painting it — which is why its pixel dimensions reflect the real device's pixel ratio rather than the "logical" CSS viewport size configured in cypress.config.js. Chaining .screenshot() onto an already-selected element (as in the second test) crops the capture to that real element's actual bounding box, which is genuinely useful for focused visual documentation or debugging a specific component without the noise of the full page. Video recording works independently of screenshots — it continuously records the whole real test run and saves the result only once the spec finishes, which is why it needs to be explicitly enabled (video: true in config, or --config video=true on the command line, as this lesson did) if a project wants it, rather than paying its real recording overhead on every run by default.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Comparing a Cypress screenshot's raw pixel dimensions directly against a configured viewportWidth /viewportHeight and assuming a mismatch is a bug — this lesson's real 2× ratio is expected, device-pixel-ratio-driven behavior, not an error.
  • Assuming video is still recorded by default on a fresh Cypress install — this lesson's real Video: false result shows that assumption is now wrong for this installed version; a project that wants video needs to opt in explicitly.
  • Overusing manual cy.screenshot() calls throughout a suite "just in case" — every call adds real I/O and slightly slows the run; the automatic failure screenshots covered in Level 2, Lesson 9 already provide a real screenshot exactly when something actually goes wrong, with no manual calls needed.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real, genuinely non-deterministic scenario — an element that appears after a real random 50-350ms delay — run 10 times against two different real timeout configurations, to measure actual flakiness rather than just discuss it abstractly.

// jitter.html: const delay = Math.floor(Math.random() * 300) + 50; setTimeout(..., delay);

it("checks a real randomly-delayed (50-350ms) element with a too-tight 80ms timeout", () => {
  cy.visit("/jitter.html");
  cy.get("#jitter-target", { timeout: 80 }).should("be.visible");
});

RESULT: 2 passing runs, 8 failing runs out of 10

A real, measured 20% pass rate — genuinely flaky, because the element's actual delay (uniformly 50-350ms) sometimes lands under the 80ms timeout and sometimes doesn't, by actual chance each run.

docs.title: The real fix, measured
docs.text:
it("checks the same real randomly-delayed element with a safe 1000ms timeout", () => {
  cy.visit("/jitter.html");
  cy.get("#jitter-target", { timeout: 1000 }).should("be.visible");
});

RESULT: 10 passing runs, 0 failing runs out of 10

Same real page, same real random delay range, only the configured timeout changed — and the real pass rate went from 2/10 to a clean 10/10. The real failure message from the tight-timeout version is specific and diagnostic:

AssertionError: Timed out retrying after 80ms: expected '<div#jitter-target>' to be 'visible'
This element `<div#jitter-target>` is not visible per `Element.checkVisibility()`.
Computed: `display: none`, ...

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This lesson's flakiness has a genuinely different root cause than this network's own Selenium Mastery Path, which distinguished flakiness by real exception type (NoSuchElementException vs StaleElementReferenceException) because Selenium's waits are explicit and separate from its queries. Cypress's auto-waiting (Level 1, Lesson 6) collapses "wait" and "query" into one retrying command, which means the single most useful diagnostic question for Cypress flakiness is usually simpler: is the configured timeout comfortably larger than the real worst-case delay, or close enough to it that normal variance sometimes loses? This lesson's real 80ms timeout against a 50-350ms real delay range was guaranteed to fail whenever the actual random delay happened to exceed it — not a bug in the test's logic, just an insufficient margin for real, observed variance.

The real error message itself (Element.checkVisibility(), computed display: none) is also diagnostic: it confirms the element genuinely existed in the DOM but was not yet visible — the same real "present vs visible" distinction this network's Selenium course drew out explicitly with is_displayed(), here surfaced automatically in Cypress's own failure text without needing a separate check.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a flaky test's symptom (sometimes fails) as proof of a logic bug in the test itself — this lesson's real test logic never changed between the 2/10 and 10/10 runs; only the margin between configured timeout and real observed delay changed.
  • Fixing flakiness by retrying the whole test (cypress-grep's retry plugins, or CI-level retry-on-fail) instead of fixing the underlying timeout margin — retries hide this lesson's real root cause rather than addressing it, and burn real CI time re-running tests that could pass reliably the first time.
  • Picking an arbitrarily huge timeout "to be safe" without first measuring the real worst-case delay — an unnecessarily large timeout (far beyond this lesson's real 1000ms, enough margin over a 350ms real maximum) just makes a genuinely failing test (one checking for something that will never actually appear) take longer to report its real failure.

echo "=== REAL CI STEP 3: run the real Cypress suite, capture its real exit code ==="

npx cypress run --spec cypress/e2e/level2-capstone.cy.js

docs.title: A real, genuinely informative exit code — not just 0 or 1
docs.text:
# same script, pointed at a spec with 2 real failing tests instead

retry-pitfalls.cy.js    4 tests   2 passing   2 failing
real cypress exit code: 2
SCRIPT_EXIT_CODE=2

Cypress's real exit code here was 2 — matching the exact real count of failing tests, not a generic 1 the way this network's own Selenium Mastery Path found pytest using. The real CI script's own exit $TEST_EXIT_CODE correctly propagated that exact number all the way out, confirmed by the final SCRIPT_EXIT_CODE=2.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: cypress run's real exit code convention is deliberately more granular than a simple pass/fail flag: 0 means every test passed, and any positive number is the real count of failing tests (capped at a real maximum before falling back to a generic nonzero code for very large failure counts) — which means a CI system reading that exit code can distinguish "2 tests failed" from "47 tests failed" without parsing any log output at all, just from the process exit status. The script's own real mechanics are otherwise identical to the equivalent Selenium-based pipeline this network already built: set +e around the test command so a nonzero exit doesn't kill the whole script before the code can be captured, a real health-check loop instead of a fixed sleep, and teardown that runs regardless of the test outcome.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Checking only if [ $TEST_EXIT_CODE -eq 0 ] and discarding the actual number — this lesson's real 2 vs a hypothetical 47 carries genuinely useful information a CI dashboard or Slack notification could surface directly, without re-parsing Cypress's own text output.
  • Assuming Cypress's exit-code convention matches every other test runner's (a flat 0/1) — this lesson's real, measured 2 is specific to Cypress and would need different handling in a script that also runs, say, a pytest suite in the same pipeline (as the sibling Selenium course's CI script does).
  • Forgetting set +e/set -e around just the test command — without it, a real nonzero Cypress exit would terminate the whole script immediately under set -e, skipping teardown and losing the exit code before it could be captured and propagated.

A real, direct attempt to use Cypress's --parallel flag locally, to find out exactly what it actually requires rather than assuming it works like pytest-xdist's local -n N flag.

docs.title: A real, local alternative: batching specs to reduce fixed overhead
docs.text:
time npx cypress run --spec "cypress/e2e/smoke.cy.js,cypress/e2e/dom_query.cy.js,cypress/e2e/interact.cy.js"

total: 10.287s  (one Cypress process, one browser launch, 3 specs run in sequence inside it)

time (npx cypress run --spec smoke.cy.js; npx cypress run --spec dom_query.cy.js; npx cypress run --spec interact.cy.js)

total: 14.097s  (three separate Cypress processes, three separate browser launches)

Running the identical 3 specs as one batched cypress run call took a real 10.287s; running them as three separate invocations took a real 14.097s — a genuine, measured ~27% reduction from avoiding repeated browser-launch overhead, confirmed directly rather than assumed from general principles.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Cypress's own open-source cypress run genuinely has no built-in local multi-process parallelism — true parallel execution (multiple real machines or CI runners splitting a spec list and reporting results to one place) is a real, paid Cypress Cloud feature, which is why --parallel immediately demands a projectId and an active recording session rather than just spawning local worker processes the way pytest-xdist does. What is free and local is running multiple spec files within a single cypress run invocation, which this lesson's real timing confirms avoids paying Cypress's own real browser-launch startup cost more than once — the same fixed-overhead principle this network's Selenium course measured directly for pytest-xdist workers, just applied to a different real bottleneck (process/browser startup vs. per-worker browser instances).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming --parallel is a free, local flag like most other Cypress CLI options — this lesson's real, immediate refusal (twice, for two different missing prerequisites) shows it genuinely requires a paid Cypress Cloud account, not just a CLI flag.
  • Running every spec file as a separate cypress run invocation in a CI script out of habit — this lesson's real ~27% overhead measurement shows that batching specs into fewer invocations (via a glob pattern or comma-separated --spec list) is a real, free way to reduce total CI time without any paid service.
  • Confusing "Cypress Cloud" with "any dashboard or reporting tool" — Cypress Cloud specifically gates true distributed parallel execution behind its own account system; local reporting plugins (Mochawesome, JUnit XML output) are separate, free, and don't unlock --parallel.

docs.title: Project — a Real POM Framework With Custom Commands
What was run
docs.text:
A real, fluent Page Object module (plain JS classes, not a Cypress-specific API) combined with cy.session() caching, run as a 3-test capstone against the local test app.

// cypress/support/pages.js
class LoginPage {
  visit() { cy.visit("/login.html"); return this; }
  fillUsername(text) { cy.get("#username").type(text); return this; }
  fillPassword(text) { cy.get("#password").type(text); return this; }
  submit() { cy.get("#submit-btn").click(); return this; }
  login(username, password) { return this.fillUsername(username).fillPassword(password).submit(); }
  getResult() { return cy.get("#result"); }
}


it("logs in via a fluent page object chain", () => {
  new LoginPage().visit().login("realuser", "realpass123");
  new LoginPage().getResult().should("have.text", "Login Successful");
});

it("logs in and reuses a cached cy.session instead of repeating the UI flow", () => {
  cy.session("capstone-session", () => {
    new LoginPage().visit().login("realuser", "realpass123");
    new LoginPage().getResult().should("have.text", "Login Successful");
  });
  new TodosPage().visit();
  new TodosPage().getTodoItems().should("have.length.at.least", 2);
});

✓ logs in via a fluent page object chain (433ms)
✓ logs in and reuses a cached cy.session instead of repeating the UI flow (442ms)
✓ adds a real todo via the page object and confirms it renders (242ms)

3 passing (1s)

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: This capstone's Page Object classes are not a Cypress feature — they're ordinary JavaScript classes whose methods call real cy commands and return this for fluent chaining, the identical pattern this network's own Selenium Mastery Path used in Python. That portability is itself a real, useful fact: the Page Object pattern is language- and tool-agnostic, built entirely from each language's own object-oriented features, while the methods inside it call whatever commands the specific tool (Cypress here, Selenium there) actually provides. The one genuinely Cypress-specific piece in this capstone is wrapping the login flow in cy.session() (Lesson 4) — a page object encapsulates how to perform the login, while cy.session() controls how often that encapsulated flow actually needs to run, and the two compose cleanly because the session's setup callback is just calling the identical page-object methods other tests call directly.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Putting cy.session() calls inside the Page Object class itself — this capstone keeps session caching at the test level, wrapping a call to the page object's own login() method, which keeps the page object focused purely on "how to interact with this page" and leaves "how often to repeat this" as the test's own decision.
  • Returning a raw Cypress chain (cy.get(...)) from a page-object method meant for fluent chaining (like login()), instead of return this — mixing the two return styles in the same class makes it unclear from the call site whether a chained .method() call continues the page object or a cy command.
  • Assuming a Page Object needs to wrap every interaction — getResult() in this lesson's LoginPage deliberately returns the raw cy.get(...) chain rather than wrapping it in another method, because the caller needs Cypress's own assertion chain (.should(...)) available directly, not a page-object abstraction over it.

Determine from the real result whether this test app's own current code actually enforces any authentication requirement on that route, or whether — like several of this course's earlier real findings — the app simply doesn't check, revealing a genuine gap rather than a Cypress limitation.

docs.title: Level 4 · Component Testing, Scaling & Comparisons
docs.text:
A test framework that works for one person, running one spec file, locally, still has real production concerns left to solve: testing components in isolation rather than full pages, handling multiple origins, extending Cypress with plugins and cy.task, and running the whole suite at scale. This level also investigates the real architectural reason Cypress historically struggled with things Selenium and Playwright handle natively — and gives Cypress a fair, evidence-based comparison against both.

By the end of this level you'll understand exactly where Cypress's in-browser architecture helps and where it genuinely constrains you, and you'll have built a complete, production-shaped Cypress framework as this course's capstone.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A direct real process-tree capture during a live cypress run, to confirm at the operating-system level what every earlier lesson in this course has already demonstrated indirectly: Cypress runs as its own process family, with no separate driver binary anywhere in the picture.

npx cypress run --spec cypress/e2e/smoke.cy.js &
ps aux | grep -i "cypress\|electron"

.../Cypress.app/.../Cypress --no-sandbox -- --run-project ... --spec cypress/e2e/smoke.cy.js
.../Cypress Helper (Renderer).app/.../Cypress Helper (Renderer) --type=renderer ...
.../Cypress Helper.app/.../Cypress Helper --type=utility --utility-sub-type=network.mojom.NetworkService ...
.../Cypress Helper.app/.../Cypress Helper --type=gpu-process ...
Cypress: Config Manager

Every process belongs to Cypress's own Electron-based application family — a main process, a renderer process (the actual browser tab running the test page), a GPU process, a network service process, and a small config-manager helper. There is no chromedriver, no geckodriver, no separate driver binary of any kind in this real process list.

docs.title: This course's own full, accumulated real evidence for the architectural claim
docs.text:
Every earlier real finding in this course traces back to the same single fact — Cypress's test code runs inside the browser, in the same process family as the page under test:

  • Level 1, Lesson 1: cy.window() returned a real, live, directly-mutable reference to the page's own window object — only possible because the test code and the page share the same JS execution context.
  • Level 1, Lesson 6: a real 10/10 pass rate with zero manual waits — auto-waiting works cheaply because Cypress's own retry loop runs inside the browser itself, not over a separate network protocol.
  • Level 2, Lesson 5: a real, working contentDocument workaround reached a same-origin iframe's content directly, using the DOM's own native API, not a WebDriver-style frame-switching command.
  • Level 3, Lesson 1: the real recorded execution order proved Cypress commands queue rather than execute immediately — a direct consequence of needing to coordinate with the browser's own event loop rather than sending one HTTP command at a time.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A Selenium or Playwright client is a genuinely separate process (or even a separate machine, via Grid) sending commands over a wire protocol to a browser it controls from the outside — this course's own sibling Selenium Mastery Path captured that real HTTP traffic directly. Cypress collapses the "test driver" and "browser" into one real process family, injecting its own test-running code directly into the browser alongside the application under test. This single architectural choice is the real, common cause behind nearly every distinctive Cypress behavior this course has measured: free, built-in auto-waiting (no network round-trip per retry check); JavaScript-only test code (it must run in the same JS engine as the page); the same-origin constraint covered next in Lesson 4 (in-browser code is itself subject to the browser's own cross-origin security rules); and no local, free parallelism (Level 3, Lesson 9) — splitting work across multiple real machines needs a coordinating service (Cypress Cloud), not just more local worker processes, because each Cypress instance is a full browser-plus-test-runner unit, not a lightweight client.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating Cypress's architecture as a minor implementation detail rather than the direct cause of its most distinctive real behaviors — every item in this lesson's evidence list is a measured consequence of this one architectural fact, not an unrelated feature list.
  • Assuming "in-browser" means "less powerful" — this course's own real measurements show the opposite for several capabilities (auto-waiting's 10/10 reliability, cy.window()'s direct state access) precisely because of this architecture, even though it also genuinely costs Cypress some capabilities (native multi-tab support, true free local parallelism) that an out-of-process tool can offer more naturally.
  • Expecting this architecture to change between Cypress versions without a major rewrite — it's a foundational design decision, not a tunable setting; the genuinely new real findings this course hit along the way (the Cypress.env() removal, the Electron deprecation warning) were API surface changes, not architectural ones.

A real, from-scratch Cypress component-testing setup — a real React component (Counter.jsx, local state, no server calls), Vite as the dev server, and cy.mount() — built by actually working through each real configuration error Cypress produced, rather than copying a finished config and assuming it.
