✓ increments on a real click, entirely in isolation (178ms)

docs.title: Four real, specific errors on the way to a working setup
docs.text:
Each was fixed in order, and each error message was specific enough to say exactly what was missing:

  1. "vite for your dev server, but a configuration file was not found" → added a real vite.config.js.
  2. "ENOENT: ... component-index.html" → added a real cypress/support/component-index.html.
  3. "cy.mount() must be implemented by the user" → registered Cypress.Commands.add("mount", mount) from @cypress/react in a real component support file.
  4. "No element found that matches selector [data-cy-root]" → added <div data-cy-root></div> to the real index HTML — the specific attribute Cypress's own mount helper looks for to attach the component.

None of these were Cypress bugs — each was a real, missing piece of a from-scratch setup, and each error message pointed directly at the fix.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Component testing mounts a real component directly into a real browser page Cypress controls — no cy.visit(), no server, no full application route — using a real dev server (Vite here) to compile just that one component and its dependencies on demand. cy.mount() is not a built-in Cypress command; it's a thin wrapper this lesson registered itself around @cypress/react's real mount() function, which is why step 3's error explicitly says it "must be implemented by the user" — Cypress deliberately doesn't assume which UI framework (React, Vue, Angular, Svelte) a project uses, so mounting logic is framework-specific and supplied by a small adapter package. The data-cy-root element from step 4 is simply the real DOM node that adapter looks for to attach the mounted component — ordinary React rendering, pointed at a specific real element Cypress's tooling already knows to query.

This is architecturally different from every earlier lesson in this course: there is no real Express server involved in Counter.cy.jsx at all — confirmed by the real speed difference between this lesson's component test durations (40ms, 178ms) and the full page-driven Level 1 capstone's per-test durations (458ms, 373ms, 378ms), which each pay the real cost of a full page navigation and a real server round-trip that component testing skips entirely.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming component testing requires a full backend or routing setup — this lesson's Counter component has zero server dependency, and the test mounted and verified it with none either.
  • Copying a finished cypress.config.js's component block from documentation without also creating the real supporting files (component-index.html, a mount-registering support file) it silently depends on — this lesson's own 4 sequential real errors are exactly what happens when those pieces are missing.
  • Treating component tests as a replacement for the E2E tests this course spent 3 levels building — they answer a genuinely different question (does this one component behave correctly in isolation?) than an E2E test (does the real, full user flow work end to end?); this course's real speed difference shows why component tests are faster, not why they're a strict upgrade.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real second Express server, started on a genuinely different port (localhost:5152, a different real origin from the main app's localhost:5151), to test exactly what happens when a Cypress test crosses an origin boundary — first without any special handling, then with cy.origin().

it("fails without cy.origin() when visiting a genuinely different real origin", () => {
  cy.visit("http://localhost:5151/");
  cy.visit("http://localhost:5152/");
  cy.get("#second-origin-heading").should("exist");
});

it("works correctly using cy.origin() to cross the real origin boundary", () => {
  cy.visit("http://localhost:5151/");
  cy.origin("http://localhost:5152", () => {
    cy.visit("http://localhost:5152/");
    cy.get("#second-origin-heading").should("have.text", "Second Origin Page");
  });
});

1) fails without cy.origin() ...
   CypressError: Timed out retrying after 4000ms: The command was expected to run against origin
   `http://localhost:5151` but the application is at origin `http://localhost:5152`.
   Use `cy.origin()` to wrap the commands run on `http://localhost:5152`.

✓ works correctly using cy.origin() to cross the real origin boundary (361ms)

The real error names both origins explicitly and tells you the exact fix — and the cy.origin()-wrapped version genuinely worked, in 361ms, against the real second server.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This is the real, concrete consequence of this course's own architectural thread (Level 4, Lesson 1): Cypress's test code runs inside the browser, subject to the real browser's own same-origin security boundaries, the same way any ordinary page's own JavaScript would be. After cy.visit("http://localhost:5152/") genuinely navigated the real browser tab to the second origin, Cypress's own top-level test code — still running in the context of the original origin — could no longer directly command what was happening in a different-origin page, exactly the restriction a real browser enforces on any cross-origin script access. cy.origin(url, callback) works around this by injecting the callback's commands to run inside the target origin's own context specifically, rather than trying to reach across the boundary from outside it — which is why the exact same cy.get("#second-origin-heading") call succeeds inside cy.origin() but times out waiting to "reconnect" outside it.

Selenium and Playwright don't share this specific real constraint in the same way, because their client code runs entirely outside any browser's JS context (Level 1, Lesson 1) — a wire-protocol client isn't itself bound by the same-origin policy the way in-browser code genuinely is.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a simple cy.visit() to a different real origin "just works" the way navigating in a normal browser tab does — this lesson's real timeout proves otherwise; Cypress's own command execution context doesn't automatically follow the navigation across origins.
  • Wrapping too little inside cy.origin() — only commands genuinely needed to interact with the different-origin page belong inside the callback; commands meant for the original origin (including anything using an outer-scope JS variable, which cy.origin()'s callback can't directly close over) need to stay outside it.
  • Confusing "different origin" with "different page on the same origin" — this course's own earlier multi-page navigation (cy.visit() between /login.html and /elements.html in Level 1) never needed cy.origin(), because localhost:5151 is the identical real origin throughout; the real boundary is scheme+host+port, not the specific path.

    .its("0.contentDocument.body.innerHTML")

1) fails to reach a real cross-origin iframe's contentDocument:
   CypressError: Timed out retrying after 4000ms: `cy.its()` errored because the property:
   `0.contentDocument.body.innerHTML` does not exist on your subject.

✓ confirms the same-origin workaround from Level 2 works for a same-origin iframe (41ms)

The identical code, the identical Cypress command, against two real iframes differing in exactly one way (same-origin vs. a genuinely different real server on a different port) — and the real result is completely different. The cross-origin iframe's contentDocument genuinely doesn't exist as an accessible property at all from the host page's perspective.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This isn't a Cypress limitation — it's the real browser's own, standard same-origin policy, which blocks any script (Cypress's own in-browser test code included, per Lesson 1) from reading a cross-origin iframe's contentDocument property at all. The browser doesn't even return a restricted-but-readable object; it simply refuses to expose the property, which is exactly why Cypress's own cy.its() reports it as not existing rather than reporting a permission error. Level 2, Lesson 5's workaround only ever worked because that iframe happened to be same-origin — this lesson closes the loop that lesson left open, confirming with a genuinely different real origin exactly where that workaround's limit is.

cy.origin() (Lesson 3) doesn't help here either, despite also dealing with cross-origin boundaries — cy.origin() lets Cypress's own test commands run inside a different origin's context after a full page navigation; it has no mechanism for reading into a live cross-origin iframe embedded within the current page, because the browser's own security model draws that line at the DOM property level, not at the level of which Cypress API you call.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming any contentDocument-based workaround generalizes to all iframes — this lesson's own real, side-by-side comparison shows it depends entirely on whether the iframe is same-origin, not on anything about how carefully the workaround code is written.
  • Reaching for cy.origin() to solve a cross-origin-iframe problem — it solves a different real problem (commands after a full navigation to a different origin), not reading into an embedded iframe from the page that contains it.
  • Treating this as something a plugin can cleanly fix — cross-origin iframe content inspection is blocked by the real browser's own security model; a plugin can at best offer narrow workarounds (postMessage bridging the frame itself implements, or testing the iframe's content as its own separate page via a direct cy.visit()), not a general bypass.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real Node-side task, registered via setupNodeEvents in cypress.config.js, that writes to the actual terminal and performs a genuine filesystem read/write — both things Cypress's in-browser test code (Level 4, Lesson 1) cannot do directly, confirmed by actually running them rather than assuming the capability boundary.

// cypress.config.js
setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
  on("task", {
    logToRealTerminal(message) {
      console.log("REAL TASK LOG:", message);
      return null;
    },
    writeRealFile({ path, contents }) {
      fs.writeFileSync(path, contents);
      return null;
    },
    readRealFile(path) {
      return fs.readFileSync(path, "utf8");
    },
  });
  return config;
},

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
setupNodeEvents runs in the real Node.js process behind Cypress — the same real process this course has confirmed, via process inspection in Lesson 1, sits alongside (but separate from) the browser's own renderer process. on("task", {...}) registers real Node functions that cy.task("name", arg) can invoke from a test, crossing from the browser's sandboxed JS context into genuine, unrestricted Node code — real filesystem access, real database queries, real console.log output to the actual terminal, anything a plain Node script could do. This is the real, structural reason cy.task() exists at all: Cypress's own in-browser commands are deliberately sandboxed the same way any browser tab's JavaScript is, and cy.task() is the one sanctioned bridge back out to the unrestricted Node environment for the specific, narrow set of things a test genuinely needs that a browser can't do on its own.

This also explains a real, useful contrast with cy.log(): cy.log() writes to Cypress's own in-browser command log, visible in the interactive Test Runner's UI, but it never appears in a cypress run terminal session the way this lesson's cy.task() output does — confirmed throughout this course's earlier lessons, where cy.log() calls never once showed up in any captured terminal output.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reaching for cy.log() when debugging a headless cypress run and being confused that nothing prints to the terminal — this lesson's real result shows cy.task() with a Node-side console.log is the correct tool for that, not cy.log().
  • Putting heavy real logic (complex data transformation, slow real I/O) directly inside setupNodeEvents without considering it blocks that one Node process — a real task that's genuinely slow (a large file write, a real database migration) adds that real time to every test that calls it.
  • Forgetting that cy.task() arguments and return values must be serializable — functions, DOM nodes, or other non-JSON-safe values can't cross the real boundary between the browser context and the Node process the way this lesson's plain strings and objects did.

docs.text:
Two real, independent ways to measure page performance from inside a Cypress test: the browser's own Navigation Timing API (reached directly via cy.window(), logged out through cy.task() from Lesson 5 since cy.log() doesn't print to the terminal), and Cypress's own reported command duration for a command that genuinely has to wait on a real server delay.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The Navigation Timing API (window.performance.getEntriesByType("navigation")[0]) is a real, standard browser API exposing precise timestamps for every phase of a page load — this course's own in-browser architecture (Lesson 1) makes it trivially reachable via cy.window(), no different from reading any other real property off the live window object. Cypress's own per-command duration, visible in every test run's output throughout this course, is a second, independent real measurement: it's simply how long that specific command took to resolve, which for a command chained after a slow real network request (cy.get("#slow-result") waiting on the page's own fetch("/api/slow")) directly reflects that real server-side delay, the same way this course's earlier Level 3, Lesson 6 incidentally reported real command timings without this lesson's dedicated focus on them.

Combining both gives two different, legitimate performance signals: Navigation Timing answers "how did the real browser's own page-load lifecycle play out," while Cypress's command duration answers "how long did waiting for this specific real condition actually take" — the second being generally more directly useful for a test suite's own performance budget, since it measures exactly what the test itself depends on.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reaching for cy.log() to print a measured timing value during a headless cypress run, then wondering why it never appears in CI logs — this lesson's own real result (confirmed again from Lesson 5) is that cy.task() with a Node-side console.log is what actually surfaces in the terminal.
  • Treating Cypress's reported command duration as a precise measurement of the real server's own response time — it includes real browser-side overhead (DOM rendering, Cypress's own retry-checking) on top of the actual network/server delay, which is why this lesson's 2048ms is slightly higher than the server's exact 2000ms, not lower or identical.
  • Using Navigation Timing metrics to measure something that happens after the initial page load (like this course's own dynamically-appearing elements from Level 1, Lesson 6) — loadEventEnd reflects the initial load lifecycle only, not any later, client-side-triggered async behavior.

docs.title: Cypress vs Selenium: a Real, Honest Comparison
What was run
docs.text: No new code — a direct comparison built from two real sources: this course's own 40 lessons of measured Cypress behavior, and this network's sibling Selenium Mastery Path's own 40 lessons of measured Selenium behavior, both run against conceptually similar real local test apps.

docs.title: Where this course's own real findings show Cypress's genuine strength
docs.text: Level 1, Lesson 6 measured a real 10/10 pass rate with zero manual waits against a 1.5s-delayed element — the exact opposite of the Selenium course's own real 15/15 failures under the equivalent zero-wait condition. Level 2, Lesson 3 and Level 3, Lesson 5 demonstrated cy.intercept()'s real network control — stubbing, spying, delaying, and dynamically responding to real requests — a capability Selenium has no comparable built-in equivalent for (it operates at the WebDriver protocol level, with no native concept of intercepting the browser's own network layer). Level 2, Lesson 9 found every single failure across this entire course auto-captured a real screenshot with zero configuration, whereas the sibling Selenium course needed a hand-written conftest.py hook (and discovered the hard way, in its own Level 3, that such a hook only works when placed in exactly the right file) to get the same real capability.

docs.title: Where this course's own real findings show Selenium's genuine strength
docs.text: Level 3, Lesson 9 found Cypress's --parallel flag genuinely refuses to run at all without a paid Cypress Cloud account and projectId — the sibling Selenium course's own pytest-xdist-based parallel execution ran entirely locally and for free, with a real measured 1.67x speedup once the suite's per-test cost was large enough. Level 1, Lesson 9 and the Selenium course's own Level 3 both independently hit a real Firefox failure in this specific sandboxed environment — but Selenium's broader language-binding support (the WebDriver protocol it speaks is implementable from Python, Java, C#, Ruby, and more) and its decade-old Grid architecture (confirmed directly from the real installed selenium-server binary's own --help output) remain real, mature capabilities Cypress's JavaScript-only, Cloud-gated-parallelism model doesn't match.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Every row in that table traces back to the same single architectural fork this course identified in Level 1, Lesson 1 and Level 4, Lesson 1: Cypress runs test code inside the browser; Selenium runs it outside, talking over a real wire protocol. Every one of Cypress's real advantages measured in this course (auto-waiting, cy.intercept(), automatic screenshots) is a direct, structural consequence of being inside the browser's own process and event loop. Every one of Selenium's real advantages (free local parallelism, broad language support, Grid) is a direct consequence of being a separate, protocol-driven client that doesn't care what language it's written in or how many separate browser processes it talks to.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Picking a side based on a single measured number (like this course's own dramatic 10/10 vs 15/15 auto-waiting contrast) without weighing the real tradeoffs this lesson's full table shows — Cypress's real Cloud-gated parallelism is a genuine, serious limitation for a large suite that Selenium's course doesn't share.
  • Assuming either tool's real, measured limitations are permanent technical ceilings rather than current product decisions — Cypress's parallel-execution gating is a business model choice, not an architectural necessity the way the in-browser/out-of-process split actually is.
  • Treating this comparison as exhaustive — Lesson 8 covers Cypress against a third, more architecturally similar tool, which surfaces a different, narrower set of real tradeoffs than this Selenium comparison does.

docs.title: Cypress vs Playwright: a Real, Honest Comparison
What was run
docs.text: No new code — a direct comparison built from this course's own real, measured Cypress findings and Playwright's publicly documented architecture, since Playwright is a genuinely closer architectural relative to Cypress than Selenium is, and the real points of difference are narrower and more specific.

docs.title: Where the two tools are genuinely similar — and this course's real evidence shows why
docs.text: Both Cypress and Playwright build in automatic waiting/retrying as a core design principle, in sharp contrast to Selenium's explicit-wait model (confirmed by this course's own real 10/10 zero-wait pass rate in Level 1, Lesson 6, versus the sibling Selenium course's real 15/15 failures under the same condition). Both also support intercepting and controlling real network traffic as a first-class feature — this course's own cy.intercept() deep dive (Level 3, Lesson 5) demonstrated stubbing, spying, and dynamic responses; Playwright's own documented page.route() offers conceptually the same real capability. Neither tool needs a separate driver binary the way Selenium does — this course confirmed Cypress's own real process tree contains no chromedriver-equivalent (Level 4, Lesson 1); Playwright similarly talks to each browser via its own native automation protocol rather than a generic WebDriver layer.

docs.title: Where the real, measured architecture actually differs
docs.text:
The one load-bearing difference this course can measure directly: Cypress's test code runs inside the browser, in the same process family as the page under test (confirmed via real process inspection in Level 4, Lesson 1), while Playwright's client runs outside the browser, communicating over each browser's own native protocol (CDP for Chromium, and equivalents for Firefox/WebKit) from a separate Node (or Python, Java, .NET) process — architecturally closer to Selenium's out-of-process model than to Cypress's in-browser one, even though Playwright also auto-waits. That one difference is the direct, real cause of several contrasts this course measured firsthand:

  • Language support: this course confirmed Cypress is JavaScript/TypeScript-only, a direct consequence of test code needing to run in the browser's own JS engine. Playwright, being an external client speaking a protocol, offers official bindings in Python, Java, .NET, and JS/TS — the same real reason Selenium supports many languages.
  • Multi-origin and multi-tab handling: this course's own real cy.origin() investigation (Lesson 3) and cross-origin iframe limitation (Lesson 4) are both direct, measured consequences of Cypress's in-browser code being subject to the real browser's own same-origin policy. An out-of-process client isn't bound by that same constraint in the same way, which is part of why Playwright's documented multi-tab and multi-context support is less encumbered by it.
  • Parallelization: this course's own real finding that --parallel is gated entirely behind a paid Cypress Cloud account (Level 3, Lesson 9) is a Cypress-specific business decision, not shared by Playwright, whose documented sharding (--shard) runs locally and freely, closer to the pytest-xdist model this network's Selenium course measured directly.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Playwright is best understood as occupying a real middle position this course's own evidence maps out precisely: it adopted Cypress's "auto-wait by default" philosophy (measured here as a dramatic real reliability win over Selenium's explicit-wait model) while keeping Selenium's "client runs outside the browser" architecture (which is what gives it multi-language support and locally-free parallelism that this course's own Cypress measurements show are genuinely constrained here). Neither tradeoff is free: this course's own real findings show Cypress's in-browser model buys auto-waiting and automatic screenshot-on-failure cheaply, but pays for it with same-origin constraints and JS-only test code — exactly the kind of genuine, measured tradeoff a tool positioned differently in the same design space would be expected to handle differently.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming "Playwright has auto-wait too" means it's architecturally identical to Cypress — this course's own real same-origin and multi-language findings show the underlying client/browser relationship is genuinely different, even though the waiting philosophy converged.
  • Treating Cypress's real Cloud-gated parallelism limitation as something Playwright also shares just because both are "modern" tools — this course's own measured finding is specific to Cypress's business model, not a shared architectural trait.
  • Choosing between the two based only on this comparison's table-level summary rather than this course's own cited, measured evidence for each row — the real lessons behind each claim ( Lesson 1, Lesson 3, Lesson 4, Level 3, Lesson 9) are what make this comparison verifiable rather than a secondhand opinion.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: No new code — a catalog of real anti-patterns, each one tied directly to a genuine bug or surprising behavior this course actually hit and investigated earlier, rather than invented hypothetical examples.

docs.title: 1. Passing an empty string to .type()
docs.text: Level 2, Lesson 2's fixture-driven login test genuinely crashed on its very first run: `cy.type()` cannot accept an empty string. The anti-pattern: assuming any string value from a data source is always safe to pass to .type() without checking for the empty case.

docs.title: 2. Breaking retry-ability with a plain .then() before .should()
docs.text: Level 3, Lesson 3 measured this directly: .invoke("text").then((t) => parseInt(t)).should("eq", 5) genuinely failed, even with .should() chained right after the .then(), because the plain callback in between doesn't retry. The anti-pattern: assuming any .should() later in a chain makes the whole chain retry-safe.

docs.title: 3. Assuming cy.intercept() applies to cy.request()
docs.text: Level 3, Lesson 5 found the identical intercept handler had zero effect on a cy.request() call — the real server genuinely answered it directly with a real 401 — while fully controlling the same logical request made through the real browser. The anti-pattern: forgetting that cy.request() bypasses the browser's network layer entirely, which is exactly what cy.intercept() watches.

docs.title: 4. Trusting a DOM alias to behave like a cached Selenium WebElement
docs.text: Level 3, Lesson 2 confirmed cy.get("@alias") re-queries the DOM fresh each time, rather than erroring on a stale reference the way Selenium's StaleElementReferenceException does. The anti-pattern: assuming an alias will fail loudly if the original element is gone, when it may instead silently resolve to a different real element matching the same underlying query.

docs.title: 5. Using cy.pause()/cy.debug() and expecting them to do anything in cypress run
docs.text: Level 2, Lesson 9 confirmed directly: cy.pause() completed in a real 217ms under headless cypress run, with zero stalling. The anti-pattern: assuming these interactive-mode-only tools have any effect outside cypress open.

docs.title: 6. Copying Cypress.env() snippets from older tutorials or training data
docs.text: Level 2, Lesson 7 hit a real, immediate removal error: `Cypress.env()` was removed in Cypress version 16.0.0, and even the replacement cy.env() needed a different real signature (an array of keys) than older documentation describes. The anti-pattern: trusting remembered or AI-generated API usage without checking it against the actually-installed version.

docs.title: 7. Assuming --parallel works like pytest-xdist's -n
docs.text: Level 3, Lesson 9 found cypress run --parallel refused to run at all without --record, which itself refused without a real Cypress Cloud projectId. The anti-pattern: assuming every modern test runner's "parallel" flag is a free, local feature.

docs.title: 8. Forgetting the same-origin constraint applies to Cypress's own test code
docs.text: Level 4, Lesson 3 and Lesson 4 both confirmed real failures — a command timeout after crossing origins without cy.origin(), and a contentDocument read that genuinely "does not exist" against a cross-origin iframe. The anti-pattern: treating Cypress's in-browser test code as exempt from the same security boundaries any other in-page JavaScript faces.

docs.title: 9. Clicking a disabled element and assuming it behaves like Selenium's silent no-op
docs.text: Level 1, Lesson 4 found Cypress's .click() on a real disabled button genuinely refuses after retrying ~4 seconds, with a specific error — the opposite of Selenium's own silent no-op on the identical element. The anti-pattern: assuming a behavior verified in one tool automatically transfers to a different one that happens to look similar.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Every entry above traces back to the same root cause this course has repeated since Level 1: Cypress will do exactly what its real, current version actually does — not what an older tutorial, a different tool's convention, or an assumption carried over from Selenium or plain JavaScript predicts. Several of these anti-patterns (3, 4, 9) are specifically about assuming Cypress behaves like Selenium when it architecturally doesn't; several others (1, 2, 6, 7) are about assuming documentation or memory is current when the actually-installed version has moved on. This course's own repeated methodology — run the real thing, read the real result, investigate when it's surprising — is the direct antidote to every anti-pattern on this list, because each one was caught by exactly that process.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating this list as exhaustive — it covers the real bugs this specific course hit; a different application under test, or a future Cypress version, will surface its own different real surprises using the identical investigative method.
  • Memorizing the fixes without the underlying mechanism — e.g. remembering "use cy.env([...]) with an array" without understanding why the API changed, which won't help diagnose the next breaking change in a future version.
  • Assuming anti-patterns only matter at scale — several of these (the empty-string .type() crash, the disabled-button assumption) were real, first-run surprises in a single test, not failures that only appear under load.

What was run
docs.text:
A real, 4-test capstone combining every major technique from this 40-lesson course into one suite: fluent Page Objects, cy.session() caching, fixture-driven data, cy.intercept() request verification, and cy.task() terminal logging — then run through this course's own real CI pipeline script to confirm the whole stack reports correctly end to end.

const { LoginPage, TodosPage } = require("../../support/pages");
